records.text:
Your Hair Loss Has Nothing to Do With Being Over 60 (It Starts in Your Gut)
Thinning hair after 60, hair falling out in the shower, or a wider part than before? Hair loss in older women and men is often blamed on age, but the real cause can start in your gut and stomach: your body may not be absorbing the iron, protein and vitamin B12 your hair needs to grow.
In this video, you’ll learn how your morning tea or coffee can block iron absorption at breakfast, and the simple breakfast swap that helps. We explain why low stomach acid after 60, heartburn pills (PPIs) and metformin can lower iron and B12, why hair shedding often starts months after surgery or illness (telogen effluvium), and how low protein, thyroid problems and biotin supplements can affect hair loss and your blood test results.
You’ll also get easy home tips for thinning hair: gentle washing, a 5-minute scalp massage, rosemary oil, protective hairstyles, and protein-rich breakfast ideas for seniors. We finish with the 3 blood tests to ask your doctor for (ferritin, thyroid TSH and vitamin B12) and a realistic 90-day plan for healthier, fuller hair after 60.


Research referenced in this video:
Hurrell et al., British Journal of Nutrition, 1999: Inhibition of non-haem iron absorption by tea, coffee and other polyphenol-containing beverages
Russell, Tufts University / NIH: Atrophic gastritis in about 1 in 5 adults over 60 and its effect on vitamin B12
Bauer et al., PROT-AGE Study Group, 2013: Protein needs of older adults (1.0–1.2 g/kg per day)
U.S. FDA Safety Communication, 2017 and 2019: Biotin interference with lab tests
Telogen effluvium: hair shedding 2–4 months after surgery, illness or stress


This video is for educational purposes only and is not medical advice. Talk to your doctor before changing any medication or starting supplements.


Is it more the hair in your brush, or a wider part that worries you? Tell us in the comments, and subscribe to Senior Health Board for simple, research-based health lessons after 60.


#hairlossafter60 #thinninghair #seniorhealth #guthealth #healthyaging

subtitles.plaintext:
If your hair has been getting thinner
after 60, age is only part of the story.
For many people, the problem starts in
the stomach, in the way the body takes
iron and other nutrients out of food.
And one of the biggest reasons is a
habit almost everyone repeats at the
breakfast table every single morning.
In the next few minutes, I'll show you
exactly what that habit is and the
simple swap that helps your body hold on
to the very thing your hair has been
starving for. You won't need an
expensive shampoo or a cupboard full of
pills.
Maybe you've noticed it in the bathroom.
The comb comes away full after a shower.
There's a little nest of hair in the
drain. And under the bright light over
the mirror, your scalp shows through
along your part.
If you've started parting your hair a
little to one side so nobody notices,
you are in very good company. Millions
of people over 60 go through this and
most of them never say a word about it.
Later in this lesson, you'll also hear
about a woman named Carol whose hair
started coming out in handfuls 3 months
after a hip operation and why it waited
3 whole months to happen. And you'll
learn the three blood tests worth asking
your doctor for. Welcome to Senior
Health Board. Here, we take what the
research says about health after 60 and
put it up on the board. Plainly, slowly,
one lesson at a time. Let's start right
at the breakfast table. Your hair needs
iron to grow. Low iron is one of the
most common reasons for hair shedding in
women. And it doesn't have to be low
enough to make you anemic. So, anything
that keeps iron from getting into your
body can show up a few months later in
your hairbrush.
For most people watching this, breakfast
comes with a cup of tea or coffee. It's
one of the nicest moments of the day.
The kettle and that first warm sip are
part of how the morning begins, and
nobody wants to give that up. You don't
have to. The problem is the timing.
Tea and coffee contain natural plant
compounds called polyphenols, and these
grab hold of iron in your gut and keep
it from being absorbed. In a study
published in the British Journal of
Nutrition in 1999, researchers gave
adults a simple bread meal with
different drinks and measured how much
iron they took in.
When the drink was black tea, iron
absorption dropped by 79% to 94%
compared with plain water. Herbal teas,
cocoa, and coffee lowered it, too.
That mostly affects the kind of iron
found in plant foods, like cereal,
bread, beans, and greens, which is
exactly what a lot of breakfasts are
made of.
So, a woman can eat a bowl of
iron-fortified cereal every morning,
wash it down with two cups of strong
tea, and absorb very little of that
iron. The fix is simple. Move your tea
or coffee. Have it about an hour before
your meal or an hour after it. And with
the meal itself, have something with
vitamin C. A small glass of orange
juice, a few strawberries, a sliced
kiwi, or some tomatoes will do. Vitamin
C does the opposite of tea. It helps
your body take iron in.
There's one more breakfast habit worth
checking. If you take a thyroid pill,
levothyroxine, in the morning, coffee
can also reduce how much of it your body
absorbs. The usual advice is to take it
with plain water on an empty stomach and
wait 30 minutes to an hour before coffee
or food. Ask your pharmacist what's
right for your particular pill. And
while we're on mornings, a word about
washing your hair. Many people start
washing it less often because they see
so much hair in the drain afterward. But
washing doesn't make hair fall out.
Those hairs were already loose, and they
would have ended up on your pillow or in
your comb anyway. What does help is
being gentle. Use lukewarm water. Press
your hair dry with the towel instead of
rubbing it, and use a wide-tooth comb
because wet hair breaks more easily than
dry hair. Your morning cup is one way
iron gets lost. Your stomach can be
another.
Eating something and absorbing it are
two different things. Your stomach has
to break food down first, and it uses
acid to do that. Stomach acid helps pull
iron out of your food, and it helps
release vitamin B12 from the protein
it's attached to in meat, fish, eggs,
and milk.
As we get older, many stomachs make less
acid. In some people, the stomach lining
slowly wears thinner, a condition called
atrophic gastritis, which simply means a
worn, thinner lining.
Robert Russell of Tufts University, in a
paper prepared for the National
Institutes of Health, estimated that
about one in five people over 60 has it.
Most of them have no idea because it
doesn't hurt.
Then, there are the pills.
A lot of people take a stomach pill
every day for heartburn, the kind whose
names end in prazole, like omeprazole.
These work by turning down stomach acid,
and they do that job well.
But, less acid can also mean less iron
and less B12 getting into your blood,
especially after years of use.
Metformin, the common diabetes medicine,
can also lower B12 over time.
Please don't stop any of these on your
own. They're often prescribed for very
good reasons, so talk to your doctor
before changing any medication.
What you can do is ask whether your iron
and B12 have been checked. When you've
been on one of these for a long time,
that's a perfectly reasonable thing to
ask.
So, you can have a woman who eats well,
who has her eggs and her fish, and still
runs low. Her plate is fine. The trouble
is somewhere between the plate and her
bloodstream.
Doctors measure your iron stores with a
test called ferritin, and hair can start
thinning when those stores are low, even
when your other blood counts look
perfectly normal.
Before we go on, I'd like to hear from
you.
Is it more the hair in your brush and
the drain that worries you, or the way
your part has started to look wider?
Tell me in the comments, because those
two often point in different directions,
and we'll get to both of them today. So,
why does hair react to all this, and why
does it take so long to show?
Under your scalp, there are around
100,000 tiny pockets in the skin called
follicles.
Each one is a small factory, and
together, they are some of the busiest
factories in your whole body.
The cells at the bottom of each follicle
divide faster than almost any other
cells you have.
Every hair goes through three stages.
First, it grows for several years. Then,
it rests for a few months. Then, it
falls out, and a new hair starts growing
from the same pocket. At any moment,
most of your hair is growing, and a
small part of it is resting.
That's why losing around 100 hairs a day
is perfectly normal. Those are just the
resting hairs finishing their turn.
You don't notice them most days because
they fall one or two at a time on a coat
collar or a hairbrush, and new ones are
already on the way.
Now, think about how a household handles
a tight budget. When money runs short,
you keep paying for the heating and the
groceries, and you cancel the magazine
subscription. Your body works the same
way.
When it runs low on iron, protein, or
certain vitamins, it keeps feeding your
heart, your brain, and your muscles
first.
Hair isn't needed to keep you alive, so
it's one of the first things to lose its
funding.
When that happens, a large number of
hairs are pushed out of the growing
stage and into the resting stage at the
same time.
They don't fall straight away. They sit
there for two to four months, and then
they let go together. So, the shedding
you see in the shower today is often the
bill for something that happened months
ago.
That delay is also why fixing it takes
patience.
Once the cause is put right, the
follicles go back to work, but a new
hair grows only about half an inch a
month. Most people start to see a real
difference somewhere between three and
six months.
Iron is one thing your hair factories
can run short of. The next one is
something most people over 60 don't eat
enough of without realizing it. Hair is
made almost entirely of a protein called
keratin.
So, when you don't eat enough protein,
your hair factory runs short of raw
material.
And many people over 60 eat less protein
than they think.
Appetite gets smaller with age. Chewing
meat can be harder. Cooking for one
doesn't always feel worth the trouble.
Breakfast turns into tea and toast,
lunch is a bowl of soup, and the only
real protein of the whole day comes at
dinner.
An international group of experts, the
PRO AGE study group, looked at this in
2013
They recommended that people over 65 get
more protein than younger adults, at
least 1.0 to 1.2 g for every kilogram of
body weight each day.
For someone who weighs 150 lb, that
works out to roughly 70 to 80 g a day.
How much is that on a plate?
An egg has about 6 grams. A small pot of
Greek yogurt has around 15.
A piece of chicken or fish about the
size of your palm has around 25.
A good aim is to have some protein at
every meal instead of saving it all for
dinner.
Add an egg or a yogurt to breakfast. Put
beans, a tin of tuna, or a slice of
cheese into lunch.
If chewing is the problem, soft foods
count just as well. Scrambled eggs,
cottage cheese, flaky fish, lentil soup,
and a smoothie made with milk or yogurt
are all easy on the teeth.
There's a small thing that helps from
the outside, too.
Many women who grew up with rollers and
tight buns still pull their hair back
tightly every day.
Constant pulling on the same roots can
thin the hair along the hairline over
the years.
Looser styles, soft scrunchies instead
of tight elastic bands, and giving the
rollers a rest a few days a week all
take the strain off those follicles.
And if you use a hair dryer, the cooler
setting is much kinder than the hottest
one. If you've ever looked for help with
thinning hair at the pharmacy, you've
almost certainly seen biotin.
It's on shelves everywhere, often in
hair, skin, and nails gummies with
pretty labels.
Biotin is a B vitamin, and a true
shortage of it can cause hair loss.
But a real biotin deficiency is rare in
people who eat a normal diet.
For most people, taking extra biotin
doesn't grow extra hair.
There's also a safety problem with high
doses, and it has to do with blood
tests.
Some of these supplements contain up to
thousands of times the amount you need
in a day.
All that extra biotin in your blood can
throw off certain lab tests, including
thyroid tests and a test called
troponin, which hospitals use to check
for a heart attack.
In 2017, the FDA warned about this after
a report of a patient taking high-dose
biotin who died after a troponin test
came back falsely low.
In 2019, the agency repeated the warning
because the problem still hadn't gone
away.
Ray is 73, a retired carpenter from
Ohio.
His daughter bought him a bottle of Hair
Gummies for his birthday, mostly as a
joke about his thinning crown, and he
took them faithfully.
A few months later, his routine thyroid
test came back looking strange, and his
doctor started talking about changing
his dose.
Before she wrote anything, she asked him
one simple question.
"Are you taking any supplements?"
Ray mentioned the gummies with a laugh.
She had him stop them for a few days and
repeated the test. It came back normal.
So, if you take biotin, tell your doctor
before any blood test and ask whether
you need it at all.
Many labs suggest stopping it for a
short time before testing, but check
first because the right gap depends on
your dose.
Your thyroid is a small gland at the
front of your neck, shaped like a
butterfly.
It sets the speed of almost everything
in your body, including how fast your
hair factories work.
When the thyroid slows down, which
doctors call hypothyroidism,
hair can become thin and dry all over
the head, and the outer ends of the
eyebrows can thin out, too.
An underactive thyroid is common after
60, especially in women, and it's easy
to miss because the other signs look
like ordinary aging.
You feel cold when everyone else is
comfortable. You're tired for no clear
reason. Your skin gets dry. You put on a
little weight, and you may become
constipated.
An overactive thyroid can thin the hair
as well, so both directions matter. The
good news is that a simple blood test
called TSH checks it, and when thyroid
levels are brought back to normal, hair
usually recovers over the months that
follow.
While your doctor checks the inside,
there's a small habit you can try at
home that most people find relaxing. A
gentle scalp massage. Before bed, or
while you sit with the evening news, put
the pads of your fingers on your scalp,
not your nails.
Press lightly and move the skin in small
circles, working from your forehead back
to the crown, then down to the nape of
your neck. Four or five minutes is
plenty. It feels lovely, and it brings
blood to the scalp. Some people like to
add a few drops of rosemary oil mixed
into a spoonful of olive or coconut oil.
If you try that, test a little on your
arm first, because some skin reacts to
it. Has anyone ever told you that you're
always cold? If that sounds like you,
write it in the comments, and tell me
whether your thyroid has ever been
checked. Now, let's go back to Carol.
Carol is 67, a retired church secretary
from Pennsylvania.
Last spring, she had a hip replacement.
The operation went well, and within a
few weeks, she was getting around with a
cane.
Then, almost 3 months later, her hair
began coming out. There were handfuls in
the shower, and strands all over her
pillow.
Her hairdresser, who had done her hair
every Saturday morning for 20 years,
took one look and said, "Carol, what's
going on with you?"
What Carol had has a long name, telogen
effluvium. But the idea behind it is
simple.
A big shock to the body, like surgery, a
serious illness, a high fever, or a
painful loss, pushes a large number of
hairs into the resting stage at once.
Remember the factory and the household
budget.
For weeks after her operation, Carol's
whole body was busy healing her hip, so
her hair was put on hold.
Two to four months later, those resting
hairs fell out together. That's why it
waited three months.
The reassuring part is that this kind of
shedding usually settles by itself,
often within about 6 months, and the
follicles start making new hair again.
But Carol's hair wasn't settling.
When her doctor ran the three tests
we're about to talk about, her ferritin
came back low.
Carol had been taking a heartburn pill
for 9 years, and every morning she had a
bowl of cereal with two cups of strong
tea.
The surgery had started the shedding,
and low iron was keeping her hair from
coming back.
Her doctor started her on an iron
supplement.
Carol moved her tea to mid-morning,
added a small glass of orange juice to
breakfast, and began eating an egg or a
yogurt every day.
In the evenings, she gave her scalp a
few minutes of massage while she watched
her quiz shows.
Around the fourth month, the handfuls
stopped.
At 6 months, standing under that same
bright bathroom light, she saw a row of
short new hairs along her part sticking
straight up like the bristles of a
little brush.
Her hairdresser noticed them before she
did. Not every case of thinning hair
comes from inside. The most common kind
of thinning after 60 is the kind that
runs in families.
In women, it usually shows up as a wider
part on top, while the hairline in front
stays where it was.
In men, it's the familiar receding at
the temples or a thin patch at the
crown.
For women, the change in hormones after
menopause plays a big part. Many women
first notice it in old photographs or
when a grandchild looks down at them
from behind the sofa and says, "Grandma,
I can see your head."
It stings a little, but it's useful
information because this kind behaves
differently from shedding and needs a
different plan.
Fixing your iron or your protein won't
reverse this kind on its own, although
it can stop a shortage from making it
worse.
There are over-the-counter treatments
for it and prescription ones, too. So,
it's worth a conversation with your
doctor, a dermatologist, or your
pharmacist. Some signs mean you should
see a doctor soon rather than wait.
Hair falling out in round, smooth
patches.
A scalp that is red, scaly, itchy, or
sore.
Hair loss that comes with a rash.
Unexplained weight loss, fevers, or
night sweats. Or sudden, heavy shedding
a few weeks or months after starting a
new medicine.
Blood thinners, some blood pressure
pills, and several others can do this.
So, bring it up with the doctor who
prescribed it and don't stop the
medicine yourself.
So, let's put all of this together into
something you can start this week.
The first step is your doctor and three
blood tests.
Ferritin checks your iron stores. TSH
checks your thyroid. And vitamin B12
checks the vitamin your stomach may be
struggling to absorb.
You can say it in one sentence at your
next visit. "My hair has been thinning
and I'd like to have my ferritin, my
thyroid, and my B12 checked." That one
request answers a lot of questions with
a single needle.
If you take biotin, mention it before
the blood is drawn.
While you wait for the results, start
the home part. These steps are small and
safe for nearly everyone.
At breakfast, move your tea or coffee an
hour away from the meal and add
something with vitamin C.
If you take a thyroid pill, give it its
own half hour with plain water before
anything else.
At every meal, put some protein on the
plate. An egg or a yogurt in the morning
and fish, chicken, beans, or cheese at
lunch.
Choose something soft if chewing is
hard. In the bathroom, wash as often as
you like with lukewarm water. Press your
hair dry and use a wide-tooth comb.
Give tight styles and hot settings a
rest.
In the evening, spend 4 or 5 minutes on
a gentle scalp massage. Now, a word
about time so you don't give up too
early. In the first month, you probably
won't see much change in the mirror and
that's normal because your body is still
refilling its stores.
By the third month, many people notice
less hair in the brush and the drain.
Somewhere between the fourth and sixth
month, look closely along your part in
good light and you may see the same
short new hairs that Carol saw.
Hair is slow, but it does respond when
you give it what it needs.
If your tests come back normal and the
thinning keeps going, go back to your
doctor and ask about the family kind of
thinning and the TR. I'd love to know
what you'll try first. Will it be moving
your morning tea, asking for those three
tests, or the scalp massage before bed?
Write it in the comments. If you know
someone over 60 who has been worried
about their hair and hasn't said much
about it, send this lesson their way.
And if you'd like more lessons like this
one, subscribe to Senior Health Board.
This is Senior Health Board. Feed the
roots, be patient with the growing, and
I'll see you in the next lesson.

records.text:
Lost an Inch or More After 70? Your Spine Is Trying to Tell You Something

Have you lost an inch or two of height? Most people over 70 find out at the doctor's office, when the nurse measures them and the number is shorter than the one on their driver's license. Losing height after 70 is very common, but it isn't simply "getting old" or bad posture. In this lesson, we explain the real reason people shrink with age: a chain of four changes in the spine that feed each other, which is why height loss can run two to three times faster after 70.

It's not just your bones. You'll learn how your spinal discs dry out and flatten, how bone thins inside the vertebrae with osteoporosis, how hidden spinal compression fractures happen without a fall and often without pain, and how weak back muscles and a forward head posture lead to a rounded upper back, also called hyperkyphosis or a dowager's hump. We also look at what height loss can tell you about your bone health, fracture risk and overall health as you age.

Then we cover what you can do: how to measure your height at home, when to ask about a bone density (DEXA) scan, four simple posture and back-strengthening exercises for seniors, foods with protein, calcium and vitamin D for strong bones, and how to lower your risk of falls.

Research referenced in this video:
Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging – height loss with age, and how it speeds up after 70
NASA – astronauts' height change in space
International Osteoporosis Foundation – undiagnosed vertebral fractures
Lindsay R et al. JAMA, 2001 – risk of a new vertebral fracture within one year
Wannamethee SG et al. Archives of Internal Medicine, 2006 – height loss and health in older men
Watson SL et al. Journal of Bone and Mineral Research, 2018 – LIFTMOR strength training trial
U.S. Preventive Services Task Force – osteoporosis screening

This video is for education only, not medical advice. Always check any changes with your own doctor.

Has anyone in your family lost height over the years? Tell us in the comments. If this lesson helped you, subscribe to Senior Health Board and share it with someone you love who's over 60.

#osteoporosis #seniorhealth #over70 #posture #healthyaging

The nurse slides the metal bar down onto
the top of your head, glances at the
scale, and writes down a number that is
an inch shorter than the one on your
driver's license. You straighten up and
ask her to measure again. She does. Same
number. For some people, that's how they
find out. For others, it's the grandson
who used to hug them around the waist
and now rests his chin on top of their
head, or the pants that suddenly drag on
the floor, or the top shelf in the
kitchen that seems to have moved up a
few inches all on its own. Most people
shrug it off. You slump a little, you
settle a little, and that's just what
happens when you get old. The research
tells a different story. The largest
long-term study of aging in America
followed thousands of people for more
than three decades. And it found that
after 70, people lose height two to
three times faster than they did in all
the years before. Something changes
inside the body around that age. And it
isn't only posture. It's a chain of four
changes inside your back. And each one
makes the next one worse. One of those
four is happening right now in millions
of people who have no idea. Doctors
estimate that about two out of every
three cases are never found at all. And
it tells you far more about your health
than an inch on a chart. By the end of
this lesson, you'll know what's really
happening inside a shrinking spine, what
your height is telling you, and the
simple things that can slow it down at
any age. Welcome to Senior Health Board.
Here we take what the research says
about health after 60 and put it up on
the board plainly, slowly, one lesson at
a time. Let's begin. To understand why
you lose height, you first need to see
where your height comes from. Your
backbone isn't one long bone. It's a
stack of 33 smaller bones called
vertebrae piled one on top of another
from the base of your skull to your
tailbone. It looks a lot like a stack of
wooden spools, the kind thread used to
come on. Between most of those spools
sits a soft cushion called a disc.
Doctors like to describe a disc as a
jelly donut. It has a tough rubbery
outer ring and a soft center that is
mostly water. Those donuts let your back
bend and twist and they soak up the
shock every time your foot hits the
ground. One fact surprises almost
everyone. Those discs make up roughly a
quarter of the length of your spine. So
the height on the doctor's chart isn't
only bone. A good part of it is water
and cushion stacked between the bones.
And that cushion changes every single
day. When you lie down at night, the
discs soak up fluid and swell a little.
When you stand and walk all day, gravity
squeezes some of that water back out.
That's why most people are slightly
taller in the morning than at bedtime.
sometimes by close to half an inch.
Astronauts show this better than anyone.
Up in space, with no gravity pressing
down, their discs fill with fluid and
spread apart. NASA has found that
astronauts can grow up to 3% taller
during a long mission, close to 2 in for
some of them. Then they come home and
gravity takes it right back within a few
weeks. So keep this picture in mind, a
stack of spools with jelly donuts in
between. Every way you can lose height
comes down to one of two things. Either
the donuts get thinner or the spools
themselves change shape. After 70, both
start happening at once. Start with the
donuts. When you were young, the center
of each disc was packed with water, held
in place by molecules that grab onto
water like a sponge. With each passing
decade, those molecules break down and
get replaced more slowly. The center of
the doughnut dries out and flattens and
the outer ring stiffens and develops
tiny cracks. Discs also have a weakness
that most of the body doesn't. They have
almost no blood supply of their own.
Instead, they get water and nourishment
the way a sponge does by being squeezed
and released. Every time you walk, bend,
or shift your weight, the discs get
pressed and then refill. Long hours of
sitting still leave them without that
gentle pumping and they dry out faster.
A flatter disc means a shorter stack.
One disc losing a sliver of height makes
little difference, but you have more
than 20 of them, and a sliver from each
one adds up. This starts much earlier
than most people think. The Baltimore
Longitudinal Study of Aging, the study
we mentioned at the start, measured the
height of more than 2,000 people over
about 35 years. Height loss began around
age 30. Between 30 and 70, men lost a
little over an inch on average, and
women lost about 2 in. So, by the time
most people notice, the shrinking has
been going on for 40 years. What changes
after 70 is the speed. And to understand
why, we need to look inside the spools
themselves. Thinner donuts only explain
part of the story. The rest is happening
inside the spools. Bone isn't a dead
solid material like stone. It's living
tissue, and your body rebuilds it all
the time. In fact, over roughly 10
years, your body replaces almost your
entire skeleton a little at a time. You
can picture two work crews living inside
every bone. One is a demolition crew. It
cells dissolve small bits of old, worn
bone. The other is a building crew. It
cells fill those spots with fresh new
bone. For most of your life, the two
crews work at about the same pace, and
your bones stay strong. Inside each
vertebrae, the result of their work is a
honeycomb of thin bony beans, a bit like
the inside of a sponge cake. As long as
the crews stay balanced, the honeycomb
stays thick. With age, the balance tips.
The demolition crew keeps working at
full speed, but the building crew slows
down. The beams in the honeycomb get
thinner, and some disappear entirely.
From the outside, the spool looks the
same. Inside, there's more air and less
bone. For women, this speeds up sharply
after menopause when the hormone
estrogen, which helps protect bone,
drops. Men lose bone, too, just later
and more gradually. By their 70s, men's
bones are often thinning at about the
same pace as women's. About one in four
men over 50 will break a bone because of
thin bone at some point. Yet, men are
far less likely to ever be tested.
Doctors have a name for bone that has
thinned this far. They call it
osteoporosis,
which simply means porous bone. You
can't feel it. There's no pain, no
stiffness, nothing in the mirror. And
that's exactly what sets up the third
reason. Now comes the part most people
have never heard of. Even though it may
be happening inside their own back right
now. When the honeycomb inside a
vertebrae gets thin enough, the bone
can't fully carry the weight above it
anymore. It doesn't snap like a broken
arm. Instead, the front edge slowly
gives way and the bone flattens into a
wedge, thick at the back and thin at the
front. Doctors call this a vertebral
compression fracture. You could call it
a crushed spool. These fractures often
happen with no fall, no accident, and no
clear moment of pain. They can come from
something as ordinary as lifting a bag
of groceries, bending to pick up a
grandchild, or a hard cough or sneeze.
Some cause a few weeks of back pain that
gets blamed on a pulled muscle. Many
cause nothing at all. According to the
International Osteoporosis Foundation,
only about one in three spinal fractures
ever comes to medical attention. The
other two go unnoticed. So when someone
loses an inch or more of height, part of
that inch may be one or more crushed
spools that nobody ever found. Jean is
79, a retired high school shop teacher
who built half the furniture in his
house. Over about 3 years, his wife
noticed he was having trouble reaching
the top of the kitchen cabinets he had
hung himself. Gene blamed his bad back
from years of hauling lumber. When his
doctor finally sent him for an X-ray, it
showed two flattened vertebrae in the
middle of his back. Gene couldn't
remember either one happening. Stories
like jeans are why this reason matters
so much. One of these fractures is a
warning sign for the next. In a study
published in the Journal of the American
Medical Association in 2001, about one
in five women who had a new spinal
fracture had another one within the
following year. If you're still
watching, type spine in the comments and
tell me whether anyone in your family
has lost height over the years. Even a
spine with healthy bone will lose height
if nothing holds it up. That job belongs
to the muscles along your back. Running
along both sides of your spine are long
muscles called the back extensors. Their
whole job is to hold you upright against
gravity all day long. They work like the
guywires that keep a tall radio tower
standing straight. Like every other
muscle, they weaken with age when they
aren't used. And most of daily life
pulls us forward. We lean over the
kitchen counter, over the steering
wheel, over the newspaper, over a phone
or a tablet. Your head weighs about as
much as a bowling ball. When it sits
right over your shoulders, your muscles
hardly notice it. When it drifts forward
a few inches, the strain on your upper
back rises sharply, the same way a
bowling ball feels light held against
your chest and heavy held out at arms
length. Reading glasses add to it. Many
people with bif focals tip their chin up
to read through the bottom of the lens
or push their head forward to see a
screen. Look around any doctor's waiting
room and you'll see a row of heads
leaning toward the floor. You can check
yourself with a simple test. Stand with
your heels and back against a wall and
look straight ahead without tipping your
chin up. If the back of your head
touches the wall easily, your upper back
is still fairly straight. If there's a
gap between your head and the wall, your
upper back has started to round forward.
Doctors use a version of this same test
in the clinic. Over time, the rounding
becomes the new normal. Doctors call an
exaggerated rounding of the upper back
hypercyphosis.
You may know it by the older name, a
dowager's hump. A rounded back takes
inches off your height without a single
bone changing size simply because the
stack is bent forward instead of
standing straight. Now, put the four
reasons together because this is where
the speed changes. Look at the Baltimore
numbers again. Men lost a little over an
inch in the 40 years between 30 and 70.
Then they lost almost another inch in
the 10 years between 70 and 80 alone.
Women lost about 2 in in those first 40
years and then about one more inch in
just one decade. That's two to three
times faster. The reason is that the
four changes stop working separately and
start feeding each other. Flatter discs
leave less cushion between the bones.
Thinner bone means each vertebrae breaks
more easily. Weaker back muscles let you
lean forward. And when you lean forward,
your weight shifts onto the front edge
of each vertebrae, which is exactly
where compression fractures happen. So,
a forward lean puts more pressure on the
front of the spools. More pressure
brings more wedge-shaped fractures. Each
wedge tips you further forward, and
tipping further forward puts even more
pressure on the front of the next spool.
Picture an old bookshelf that has
started to lean. Every book you add
makes it lean a little more, and the
more it leans, the faster it tips. It
never straightens itself out. That's the
real reason people shrink after 70. It
isn't just gravity, and it isn't simply
bad posture. It's a chain of four
reasons that feed each other. And the
most dangerous one is the one you can't
feel. You might think an inch or two is
only a question of how your pants fit.
Researchers have found it can tell you
much more. In Britain, a large study
followed more than 4,000 men for 20
years from middle age into their 60s and
70s and published the results in the
Archives of Internal Medicine in 2006.
Men who lost more than an inch of height
over that time, about 3 cm, were 64%
more likely to die during the study than
men who lost less than half an inch.
They also had more heart disease even
after the researchers accounted for
their other health problems. Nobody is
saying height loss causes heart disease.
Think of it as a warning light on a
car's dashboard. The light itself isn't
the problem, but it's telling you
something underneath needs a look.
Faster height loss often reflects
thinning bone, shrinking muscle, and
less activity, and all three affect your
health in many other ways. A rounded
upper back can also crowd the chest and
belly. Some people notice they run out
of breath sooner or feel full after only
a few bites. And a forward lean moves
your center of balance, which makes a
fall more likely at exactly the age when
a fall is most likely to break a hip.
So, your height is one of the simplest
health measures you have. It costs
nothing, takes 10 seconds, and most
people haven't checked it in years. If
this lesson is useful so far, type the
letter H in the comments. Not everyone
loses height at the same pace. Two
sisters raised in the same house can end
up 2 in apart by the time they're 80.
Family history plays a big part. If your
mother or father lost a lot of height,
broke a hip, or developed a rounded
back, your own risk is higher because
the bone you build when you're young is
partly inherited. Smaller, thinner
people start with less bone in the bank,
so they reach the danger zone sooner.
Smoking and heavy drinking both speed up
bone loss, and so does an early
menopause. And activity matters more
than most people expect. Bone and muscle
respond to the loads you put on them.
Long stretches of sitting, weeks in bed
after an illness, or years of lifting
nothing heavier than a coffee cup all
send your body the same message. These
bones and muscles aren't needed. Your
body listens and it lets them go. The
good news is that the same rule works in
reverse. When you start asking more of
your bones and muscles, they start
answering even late in life. For years,
women with thin bones were told to avoid
strength training for fear it would
cause fractures. Then in 2018,
researchers in Australia published the
Lyftmore trial in the Journal of Bone
and Mineral Research. Women with low
bone mass, average age about 65, did
supervised strength training twice a
week for eight months. Their spine bone
density went up by almost 3% while it
went down in the group doing gentle
exercise at home.
One more result surprised even the
researchers. The strength training group
gained a little height back on average
while the other group kept shrinking.
Your spine still responds when you give
it a reason to. Five steps make a good
start. First, measure your height once a
year. Stand in your socks with your back
against a wall, heels touching the wall,
eyes looking straight ahead. Lay a hard
coverver book flat on top of your head,
pressed against the wall, and have
someone make a small pencil mark under
it. Write down the date. If you've lost
more than an inch overall or half an
inch or more in a single year, tell your
doctor. It can be a sign of a crushed
spool nobody has found. Second, know
your bones. A bone density scan, often
called a DEXA scan, takes about 10
minutes, doesn't hurt, and uses a very
small amount of X-ray. National
guidelines recommend it for women 65 and
older. If you're a man or you've already
lost height, ask your doctor whether it
makes sense for you. Third, strengthen
the muscles that hold you up. Four
simple moves at home make a good start.
The wall stand. Stand with your heels,
hips, shoulders, and the back of your
head against a wall and hold for 30
seconds. If your head won't reach the
wall, don't force it. Just get as close
as you comfortably can. The chin tuck.
Sitting tall, slide your chin straight
back as if you're making a double chin
and hold for 5 seconds. Do 10 a day. It
moves your head back over your shoulders
where it belongs. The shoulder blade
squeeze. Pull your shoulder blades back
and down as if you're holding a pencil
between them. Hold for five seconds and
repeat 10 times. The prone lift for
anyone who can safely lie on the floor
or a firm bed. Lie on your stomach with
a pillow under your hips. Lift your head
and shoulders just an inch or two, eyes
on the floor. Hold for three seconds and
lower slowly. Start with five. Skip
exercises that curl your spine forward
with force, like toe touches and
sit-ups. With thin bones, that bending
motion is exactly how a spool gets
crushed. Fourth, feed your bones. Your
building crew needs protein, calcium,
and vitamin D. Milk, yogurt, cheese,
eggs, beans, leafy greens, and canned
salmon, or sardines with the soft bones
are all good sources. Many people over
70 eat too little protein, especially at
breakfast, so add some to every meal.
Walking helps your discs, too. Each step
presses and releases them, which is
exactly the pumping they need to stay
full. A daily walk is one of the few
things that helps all four reasons at
the same time. Fifth, protect yourself
from falls because a fall is what turns
thin bone into a broken one. Walk every
day if you can. Keep your floors clear
and put nightlights between the bedroom
and the bathroom. Evelyn is 76, a
retired piano teacher who spent 50 years
bent over a keyboard. When the nurse
told her she'd lost almost 2 in, she was
more embarrassed than worried. Her bone
scan showed thin bone in her spine. So,
she did her four moves every morning
while the coffee brewed, added Greek
yogurt and a boiled egg to her
breakfast, and walked to church twice a
week instead of driving. A year later,
her height hadn't dropped any further.
Her friends kept telling her she was
standing taller. And for the first time
in years, she could reach the top shelf
of her music cabinet without a step
stool. So, back to that moment at the
doctor's office when the nurse writes
down a number shorter than the one on
your license. Most people treat that
number as a fact of age, something to
shrug off. Now you know it's a signal.
It can point to drying discs, thinning
bone, tired muscles, and sometimes a
crushed spool that nobody has found.
Every one of those reasons can be slowed
down. And the bones and muscles that
hold you up are still listening at 70,
at 80, and beyond. They still respond to
the work you give them. If someone in
your life has been getting shorter, send
them this lesson. It might lead to a
simple scan or a daily habit that
protects their back for years. Tell me
in the comments which of the four moves
you'll try first and subscribe so the
next lesson finds you. This is Senior
Health Board. Stand a little taller and
I'll see you in the next lesson.

records.channelDescription:
Welcome to Senior Health Board!
Practical, easy-to-understand health and wellness information for adults 60 and older.
On this channel, we focus on healthy aging, mobility, nutrition, sleep, heart health, everyday habits, and common health concerns that can affect quality of life as we get older.
Our goal is simple: turn complicated health topics into clear, useful information you can actually understand and apply in daily life.
No confusing medical jargon. No unnecessary fear. Just straightforward educational content designed to help you make more informed choices about your health and well-being.
Subscribe for regular videos about staying active, independent, and healthier as you age.

This channel is for educational purposes only and is not a substitute for personalized medical advice from your own phy.

records.text:
Many older adults wake up from surgery confused, frightened or “not themselves,” and families are often told it’s just age. In this video, we explain what postoperative delirium is, why the brain is more sensitive to anesthesia, pain medicine and hospital stays after 65, and why the quiet, sleepy kind of delirium is so often missed.
We count down five common mistakes people make before and after surgery. They include saying “I’m fine” when you aren’t, bringing an incomplete medication and supplement list, leaving glasses and hearing aids at home, going without water longer than needed, and spending all your questions on general vs. spinal anesthesia. Then we walk you through The Clear Mind Plan, a simple step-by-step routine for the weeks before surgery, the hospital days and the first two weeks at home. A version of this routine, with family members helping each day, cut delirium from about 1 in 5 patients to fewer than 3 in 100.
If you or someone you love has a surgery coming up, this lesson will help you prepare your body, your bag and your questions for the anesthesia team.


Research referenced in this video:
Neuman MD et al. REGAIN Trial, spinal vs. general anesthesia for hip surgery. New England Journal of Medicine, 2021.
Moller JT et al. ISPOCD1, long-term postoperative cognitive dysfunction in the elderly. The Lancet, 1998.
Makary MA et al. Frailty as a predictor of surgical outcomes in older patients. Journal of the American College of Surgeons, 2010 (Johns Hopkins).
Wang YY et al. Tailored, family-involved Hospital Elder Life Program and postoperative delirium. JAMA Internal Medicine, 2020.
American Society of Anesthesiologists. Practice Guidelines for Preoperative Fasting, 2023 update.
American Society of Anesthesiologists. Herbal and Dietary Supplements and Anesthesia.
Multi-society clinical guidance on GLP-1 receptor agonists before procedures, 2024.
American Geriatrics Society. Postoperative Delirium in Older Adults: Best Practice Statement, 2015.
American Geriatrics Society. Beers Criteria, 2023 update.

Medical disclaimer: This video is for educational purposes only and is not medical advice. Always talk to your own doctor or surgical team before changing any medication, supplement or fasting instruction.

If this lesson helped you, subscribe to Senior Health Board for clear, research-based health lessons for people over 60. Tell us in the comments: L, Q or S?

You're lying in a hospital bed the day
after your hip surgery. The doctor stops
by in the morning, smiles, and tells you
everything went perfectly. You feel
tired and a little sore, but you're
relieved. The hard part is over. Then
the second night comes. The door opens
and a woman walks in holding a bag of
oranges and a blue sweater. Her face
looks familiar, like someone you've seen
somewhere before, but you just can't
place her.
She comes closer, sets the oranges on
the table, and leans over the bed. And
then she says, "Hi, Mom." You stare at
her for a long moment, and the name
still won't come. So, you lean in and
whisper that the nurses are putting
something in your water and that you
want to go home right now. Out in the
hallway, your daughter asks the nurse
what's happening, and the nurse just
shrugs and says it's normal at her age.
The next morning, the doctor says almost
the same thing. And by the weekend, your
whole family is repeating it, too. It's
just her age. And that was it. Nobody
looked any further. And from then on,
everyone started treating you a little
differently, as if the surgery had
suddenly made you old. But what happened
that night was not just getting older.
It has a name, post-operative delirium.
It has specific causes. Many of them you
can do something about before you even
get to the hospital. And for a lot of
people, it can be prevented with steps
so simple that most families are never
told about them. And it is not rare. In
a large trial published in the New
England Journal of Medicine in 2021,
doctors followed 1,600 people having hip
surgery with an average age of 78. About
one in five developed delirium in the
days after the operation. In 1998, a
study in the Lancet tested 1,218
people over 60 after major surgery. A
week later, about a quarter had clear
memory and attention problems. And three
months later, about 1 in 10 still did.
But the number that surprised me most
came from John's Hopkins. They found one
group of older patients who were 20
times more likely to leave the hospital
for a nursing home instead of going back
to their own house. I'll tell you
exactly who was in that group in a few
minutes because it's something you can
check and change weeks before your
surgery. So, this is what we're going to
do today. First, I'll show you on the
board what actually happens to the brain
around surgery with one simple picture.
Then we'll count down the five most
common mistakes people make before and
after surgery from number five to number
one. Number one is the question almost
everybody asks before an operation and
it turns out to be the wrong place to
spend your energy. And at the end I'm
going to walk you through a simple daily
plan that was tested in a hospital on
281 older surgery patients. Delirium
dropped from about one in five people to
fewer than three in a hundred. No new
drug, no special machine, just ordinary
things a family can do, and I'll show
you everyone. But first, I'd like to ask
you something. Tell me in the comments
which one sounds like your experience.
If you or someone you love became
restless, agitated, or frightened after
a surgery, type the letter L. If it was
the opposite, very sleepy, slow, far
away, type Q. And if you have a surgery
coming up and you want to be ready, type
S. Just one letter. By the end of this
video, you'll know exactly what your
letter means. Welcome to Senior Health
Board. Here we take what the research
says about health after 60 and put it up
on the board plainly, slowly, one lesson
at a time. This is education, not
medical advice. So, always check any
changes with your own doctor. Let's
begin. I want you to think of your
brain's reserve as a bridge. Every day,
small trucks drive across it. A meal, a
conversation, a walk to the mailbox, and
the bridge carries them easily. Surgery
day is different. On surgery day, a lot
of heavy trucks try to cross at the same
time. There are the anesthesia drugs and
the sedatives. There is pain and the
strong medicine for pain. There are long
hours without food or water. There's a
night of beeping machines, often a room
where you can't see or hear well, and
sometimes an infection on top of it all.
When you're 35, the bridge is wide with
plenty of lanes and it carries all of
that. With age, the bridge gets
narrower. The brain has fewer spare
connections and it becomes more
sensitive to drugs. Things like hearing
loss, diabetes, or early memory changes
each take away a lane. So, when too much
weight arrives at once, the bridge
buckles for a while. That buckling is
delirium. It's a sudden change in
attention and clear thinking that comes
on over hours or days. It goes up and
down and it's usually worse in the
evening and at night. Doctors describe
two kinds. The first kind is loud. The
person is restless, pulls at the IV,
tries to climb out of bed, or is
convinced someone wants to hurt them
like the mother in our story. That's
your letter L, and everybody notices it.
The second kind is quiet. The person is
drowsy, slow, staring at the wall,
barely talking. Nurses may even say,
"Such an easy patient." That's your
letter Q, and it's the one that gets
missed because nobody rings a bell for
someone who's simply sleeping. And if
you typed S, you're standing in front of
the bridge before the trucks arrive. And
that's the best place to be. Every
mistake on our list adds a truck and
every part of the plan takes one off.
Mistake number five is one people make
with the best of intentions. Someone
asks how you're doing and you say, "I'm
fine." You say it to the surgeon, to the
nurse, to your own kids. Let me tell you
about a woman. We'll call her Ruth.
She's 73, a retired bank teller, and she
was getting ready for a knee
replacement. In the year before, after
her husband passed, Ruth had lost about
12 pounds without trying. She felt tired
most afternoons, and she had stopped her
morning walks. When the surgeon asked
how she was doing, she smiled and said,
"Oh, I'm fine." The surgery went well,
but afterwards, she was weak and foggy
for days and spent three weeks in a
rehab facility. This is where that
John's Hopkins study comes back. In
2010, researchers there measured 594
people over 65 before planned surgery.
They used a simple test that takes about
10 minutes called a frailty score.
[snorts] It gives one point each for
losing 10 pounds or more in a year
without trying, a weak hand grip,
feeling exhausted, very little physical
activity, and a slow walking speed. The
people who scored as frail had two and a
half times more complications after
surgery. They stayed in the hospital
longer and they were 20 times more
likely to be sent to a nursing home or
assisted living instead of going home.
That was the group I promised to tell
you about. Ruth would have scored at
least three of those five points. The
good news is that most of them can move
in a few weeks. And some hospitals now
offer a short program to build you up
first called prehabilitation.
So the fix is to be honest about your
weight, energy, walking, and memory. And
I'll give you the exact words near the
end. If you've ever told a doctor, "I'm
fine," when you weren't really fine,
type the number five in the comments.
You'll see how many people have done the
same thing. Ruth's story has one more
piece, though, and it was sitting in her
kitchen cabinet. Mistake number four is
walking into the hospital with an
incomplete medication list. Most people
bring their prescriptions and nothing
else. When Ruth's daughter cleaned out
the kitchen cabinet later, she found a
bottle of GKO for memory, a bottle of
vitamin E, a garlic supplement for her
heart, and a nighttime pain reliever
that Ruth took most evenings to help her
sleep. None of those were on her list.
To Ruth, they weren't medicine. They
were just the vitamins. The American
Society of Anesthesiologists is very
clear on this. They ask patients to tell
the team about every prescription, every
over-the-counter product, and every
vitamin and herbal supplement, even the
ones you've taken for years without any
problem.
>> [snorts]
>> Some herbs like GKO, garlic, ginsing,
and vitamin E can increase bleeding.
Others like St. John's wart, cava, and
valyan can make anesthesia drugs
stronger or last longer. That's why your

around surgery when possible. And if you

says most people can keep taking it, but

Someone else in our story did his list
perfectly. What he forgot wasn't in a
bottle at all. It was supposed to be in
his ears. Mistake number three is
leaving your glasses, your hearing aids,
or your dentures at home or letting them
disappear into a bag after surgery. Let
me tell you about Walter. He's 78, a
retired machinist, tall and thin, and
he's worn a hearing aid in his right ear
for years. Before his gallbladder
surgery, he left the hearing aid in his
dresser drawer at home because he was
afraid it would get lost in the
hospital. His glasses went into a
plastic bag with his clothes. When
Walter woke up, the nurse's questions
sounded like voices underwater, and
their faces were soft blurs. So he just
nodded and said yes to everything. By
the second night, he was trying to climb
over the bed rail because he was sure he
was late for work. Your brain figures
out where you are from small clues. A
familiar face, the clock on the wall, a
sentence it can follow. Without sight
and hearing, those clues disappear. And
in a strange room with drugs in your
system, the brain guesses wrong. This is
why the American Geriatric Society lists
glasses and hearing aids among the first
things to get right after surgery and
why hospital programs built to prevent
delirium make sure they're back on as
early as possible. So, the fix is to
bring them in a case with your name on
it. Ask the team to put them back on in
the recovery room or as soon as it's
safe. and tell your family it's their
job to check that they're on every
single visit. Bring spare hearing aid
batteries, too. If you wear glasses or a
hearing aid, type the number three in
the comments so I know you're still with
me. Number two happens before you even
leave the house, the night before
surgery, at the kitchen sink. Mistake
number two is going without water much
longer than you actually need to. Almost
everybody has heard the rule nothing to
eat or drink after midnight. Let me tell
you about Linda. She's 68 and her
surgery was scheduled for 2 in the
afternoon. She followed that old rule
exactly. She took her last sip of water
at a/4 to midnight and by the time she
reached the operating room, it had been
more than 14 hours. She arrived with a
headache, lightaded and worn out before
anything had started. The fasting rule
exists for a good reason because an
empty stomach protects your lungs during
anesthesia. But for clear liquids, the
guidance has changed. In 2023, the
American Society of Anesthesiologists
updated its fasting guideline for
planned procedures. For healthy
patients, clear liquids are generally
fine until 2 hours before surgery. Clear
liquids means water, fruit juice without
pulp, clear tea, or black coffee with no
milk. The guideline also notes that
clear drinks with some carbohydrate in
them can help with hunger. This matters
more after 60 because the older body
sends a weaker thirst signal and
dehydration is another heavy truck on
the bridge that can lower blood pressure
and make delirium more likely. So, the
fix is to ask your team exactly when
your last clear drink should be and what
you're allowed to have. Some people do
need to stop earlier, and your team's
instruction is the one that counts. Just
don't add extra hours on your own. And
now we've come to number one, the
question almost everyone asks before
surgery. Mistake number one is spending
all your questions and all your worry on
whether you'll have general anesthesia
or a spinal. Frank is 76 and at his
pre-surgery visit for a new hip, he
spent the whole time on one question.
Can I have a spinal so I don't go all
the way under? He'd read that it was
easier on the brain. What he didn't ask
about was the 3 days after. His children
lived 3 hours away. Nobody visited until
the weekend. His room stayed bright
until late at night. He barely slept and
he hardly left the bed. On day two, he
became confused and frightened. The
trial I mentioned at the start, the one
from the New England Journal of Medicine
in 2021 called Regain, tested exactly
Frank's question. It puts 1600 hip
surgery patients randomly into two
groups, spinal or general anesthesia.
Delirium happened in 20.5% of the spinal
group and in 19.7% of the general group.
That's practically the same. At two
months, the number of people who had
died or couldn't walk on their own was
also almost identical between the
groups. There can still be good medical
reasons to choose one or the other, and
that's a decision for you and your
anesthesia team. But for delirium, the
research points somewhere else. Much of
the risk is decided in the hours and
days after surgery. whether you sleep at
night, whether you see daylight, whether
you get up and move, whether you drink
and eat, and whether someone familiar is
sitting beside you. So, the question
that really changes things isn't only
spinal or general. It's also who will be
with me and what is the plan to keep my
mind clear after surgery. Before we get
to that plan, hit the like button if
this has been useful so far. And if you
haven't subscribed yet, now is a good
moment because the plan coming up is the
part you'll want to come back to before
any surgery. We call this the clear mind
plan. It has five parts and the first
one starts weeks before the hospital.
Part one is building up the bridge two
to four weeks before surgery. Walk every
day, even five or 10 minutes at first,
and add a little each week. Practice
standing up from a firm chair without
using your hands 10 times twice a day.
Eat some protein at every meal and keep
the same bedtime every night. Ruth did
exactly this before her second knee a
year later and she went in stronger than
the first time. Part two is the bag one
week before. Put every bottle in one
bag, prescriptions, vitamins, herbs, and
eye drops and bring it to your
pre-surgery appointment so the team can
tell you what to pause and when. In a
second bag, pack your glasses, your
hearing aids with spare batteries, and
your dentures with your name on
everything. Part three is the night
before. Ask exactly when your last clear
drink is allowed. Set an alarm so you
actually take it and arrange for someone
you know to be there when you wake up.
Part four is the heart of the plan, the
hospital days. And it comes from the
study I promised you. It was published
in JAMAMA internal medicine in 2020 from
West China Hospital with 281 surgery
patients average age about 75. In one
group, family members were taught a few
simple daily habits. In the usual care
group, 19.4% developed delirium. In the
family group, it was 2.6% and they went
home about 4 days sooner. What the
families did was ordinary. Every morning
they opened the curtains, put the
glasses and hearing aids on, and talked
about the date and the news from home.
They helped with eating and drinking,
and with walking as soon as the team
allowed, often on the first day. And in
the evening, they kept the room dim and
quiet so the patient could sleep. When
Frank had his other hip done the next
year, his daughter did exactly that for
3 days. He slept at night, walked the
hallway twice a day, and went home on
day four, clear, grumpy, and completely
himself. Part five is the first two
weeks at home. Keep the same rhythm,
daylight and movement in the day, a dark
room at night. Watch for the quiet kind
of delirium, too much sleeping, and not
following a conversation, and don't
start any new sleep aid without asking
your doctor. If you're going to pack
your bags this way, type the word clear
in the comments and save this video for
before the surgery. Before we finish,
there are a few signs that need
attention right away. The first is
confusion that comes on suddenly,
especially if it gets worse quickly or
comes with a fever. In the hospital,
tell the nurse right away because
delirium can signal an infection, low
oxygen, or a medicine reaction. And at
home, call your doctor the same day. If
the person is very hard to wake up, has
trouble breathing, has chest pain, or
shows signs of a stroke like a drooping
face or a weak arm, call 911. And if the
thinking problems are still there a few
weeks after surgery, don't accept it's
just age. Ask for a proper check. At
your pre-surgery visit, this is the
sentence I promised you. I'm worried
about getting confused after surgery,
and I'd like a plan to help prevent it.
A good first question after that is
whether you should have a quick memory
and strength check before the operation
so the team knows you're normal. After
that, you might ask which of your
medicines and supplements to pause and
when. And finally, you could ask whether
the hospital has a delirium prevention
program and how your family can be part
of it. That mother with the oranges and
the blue sweater wasn't suddenly old.
Her bridge was simply carrying too much
at once and most of those trucks could
have been taken off before she ever
reached the hospital. Share this video
with someone over 60 who has a surgery
coming up and subscribe because next
time we're opening the medicine cabinet
to five common pills that can raise the
risk of a heart attack or stroke. This
is Senior Health Board. Bring your
glasses, bring a person, and I'll see
you in the next lesson.

Welcome to Senior Health Board!
Practical, easy-to-understand health and wellness information for adults 60 and older.
On this channel, we focus on healthy aging, mobility, nutrition, sleep, heart health, everyday habits, and common health concerns that can affect quality of life as we get older.
Our goal is simple: turn complicated health topics into clear, useful information you can actually understand and apply in daily life.
No confusing medical jargon. No unnecessary fear. Just straightforward educational content designed to help you make more informed choices about your health and well-being.
Subscribe for regular videos about staying active, independent, and healthier as you age.

This channel is for educational purposes only and is not a substitute for personalized medical advice from your own phy.

records.text:
Cardiologist Warns: Millions Still Do This Every Morning Without Knowing the Risk!

If you're over 60, the first hours after you wake up are the hardest hours of the day for your heart. Research shows heart attacks happen most often between 6 a.m. and noon, and stroke risk climbs by about half in the same morning window. In this lesson, we explain what happens to your heart and blood pressure when you wake up: the morning surge in cortisol and adrenaline, tighter arteries, stickier platelets, and why morning blood pressure spikes become more common with age.

We count down five common morning habits that put extra strain on your heart: taking ibuprofen, naproxen or other NSAID pain relievers first thing, cold and sinus pills with decongestants that raise blood pressure, a salty breakfast of bacon, sausage and biscuits, shoveling snow or doing heavy work in the cold right after waking, skipping or delaying your morning blood pressure medication, and the habit almost everyone has: never checking your blood pressure in the morning. You'll learn about masked morning hypertension, why your doctor's office reading can look normal while your morning numbers are high, and what that means for heart attack and stroke risk.

Then you'll get the Quiet First Hour: a simple morning routine to protect your heart, including how to take an accurate home blood pressure reading, how to choose the right upper-arm cuff, when to take your blood pressure pills, a low-sodium breakfast, safe snow shoveling tips for seniors, and how to check which over-the-counter medicines are safe for high blood pressure and heart disease.

Research referenced in this video:
Muller JE et al. New England Journal of Medicine, 1985 (morning onset of heart attacks)
Elliott WJ. Stroke, 1998 (morning timing of stroke, meta-analysis)
Tofler GH et al. New England Journal of Medicine, 1987 (morning platelet stickiness)
Kario K et al. Circulation, 2003 (morning blood pressure surge and stroke in older adults)
U.S. FDA Drug Safety Communication, 2015 (NSAIDs and heart attack or stroke risk)
American Heart Association (decongestants, sodium limits, home blood pressure monitoring)
Dickinson KM et al. American Journal of Clinical Nutrition, 2011 (high-salt meal and artery function)
Auger N et al. Canadian Medical Association Journal, 2017 (snowfall and heart attacks)
Mazzaglia G et al. Circulation, 2009 (blood pressure medication adherence)
CDC – Heart disease facts

This is education, not medical advice — always check any changes with your own doctor. Talk to your doctor before changing any medication. If you have chest pain, pressure, shortness of breath or sudden weakness on one side of your body, call 911.

Which step will you start with tomorrow morning? Tell us in the comments. If this lesson helped you, subscribe to Senior Health Board and share it with someone you love who's over 60.

and it can show you the most.
Call 911 right away if you have chest
pain, pressure, or tightness, pain
spreading to your arm, jaw, neck, or
back, sudden shortness of breath, a cold
sweat, or sudden weakness or numbness on
one side of your face or body.
Women often feel heart attack symptoms
as nausea, unusual tiredness, or back
pain rather than chest pain.
Don't drive yourself. Call your doctor
soon if your morning readings are often
above 160
or if you feel chest discomfort or
unusual breathlessness that appears in
the morning and fades later in the day.
At your next visit, you can say, "I've
started checking my blood pressure in
the morning and I'd like you to look at
my numbers."
Then ask three questions.
Is my morning blood pressure where it
should be?
Is the timing of my medicine right for
my mornings?
Which over-the-counter pain or cold
medicines are safe for me?
Talk to your doctor before changing any
medication.
Tell me in the comments which step
you'll start with tomorrow morning. Then
send this lesson to someone you love
who's over 60, especially someone who
still shovels their own driveway.
If you'd like more lessons like this
one, subscribe so the next one finds
you. Next time, we'll look at the most
common mistakes people make in the
shower and the bath after 60. And the
one that sends the most people to the
emergency room.
This is Senior Health Board. Give your
heart a quiet first hour, and I'll see
you in the next lesson.

records.text:
Don’t Choose a Cataract Lens Until You Know This

Cataract surgery is one of the most common surgeries after 60, and one of the most successful. Yet many people never hear the most important part: before your operation, you have to choose an intraocular lens (IOL), and that choice shapes how you see for the rest of your life. In this video we compare the three main types of cataract lens: the standard monofocal lens, the multifocal lens and the extended depth of focus (EDOF) lens. You’ll see what each one does for reading, driving and night vision.

We walk through five common mistakes people make when choosing a cataract lens: getting measured while their eyes are dry, not telling the surgeon about macular degeneration or glaucoma, assuming the standard Medicare-covered lens is second-rate, forgetting about halos and glare when driving at night, and never saying what they actually want to see without glasses. You’ll also learn about monovision, the real cost of premium lenses, and what recovery after cataract surgery looks like in the first 30 days. That includes the eye drop mistake that 9 out of 10 patients make.

If you or someone you love is over 60 and cataract surgery is coming up, watch this before your consultation.

Research referenced in this video:
National Eye Institute – cataract prevalence by age 80
Tseng et al., JAMA 2012 – cataract surgery and hip fracture risk in Medicare patients
Lee et al., JAMA Internal Medicine 2021 – cataract surgery and dementia risk (Adult Changes in Thought study)
de Silva et al., Cochrane Review 2016 – multifocal vs. monofocal intraocular lenses
Systematic review 2022 – dry eye disease after cataract surgery (36 studies)
Review of 145 publications – dry eye and cataract surgery
Pseudophakic mini-monovision study, 2018 – 56 patients
Schlenker et al., JAMA Ophthalmology 2018 – cataract surgery and traffic crashes
Osher – negative dysphotopsia long-term study
An et al., Journal of Cataract and Refractive Surgery 2014 – eye drop errors after cataract surgery
Medicare.gov – eyeglasses after cataract surgery
This video is for education only and is not medical advice. Always check any changes with your own doctor.

Chapters:
0:00 The decision before cataract surgery
0:57 Why cataract surgery matters after 60
2:27 How the new lens works: monofocal, multifocal, EDOF
4:10 Mistake 5: Getting measured with dry eyes
6:10 Mistake 4: Keeping quiet about the rest of your eye
8:15 Mistake 3: Believing “standard” means second-rate
10:10 Mistake 2: Forgetting about your nights
12:30 Mistake 1: Never saying what you want to see
14:25 The first 30 days after cataract surgery
16:06 The Lens Talk: your plan
18:21 Red flags after surgery
18:58 What to ask your doctor
19:29 Final thoughts

Have you had cataract surgery, or is it coming up? Tell us in the comments which lens you chose or are thinking about. Subscribe to Senior Health Board for more research-based health lessons after 60.
