The #1 Old-Fashioned Food for Tired Blood After 60

Always tired after 60? Feeling worn out by the afternoon, even after a full night’s sleep? In this video, we look at blackstrap molasses, the old-fashioned black syrup that American grandmothers kept in the pantry and took by the spoonful as a tonic for “tired blood.” Blackstrap molasses is made from the third boiling of sugarcane, and one tablespoon contains iron, calcium, magnesium and potassium, minerals that many seniors and adults over 60 don’t get enough of.
We count down five benefits of blackstrap molasses for seniors: more antioxidants than honey or white sugar, minerals for bone health and osteoporosis prevention, a gentler effect on blood sugar and insulin, potassium for heart health and blood pressure, and iron for fatigue and low energy linked to iron deficiency anemia. You’ll also hear the true story of the 1950 bestseller “Look Younger, Live Longer” and why the FDA seized copies of it in 1951.
Most importantly, you’ll learn the common morning habit that blocks the iron in molasses, how to take blackstrap molasses the right way with lemon and vitamin C, a simple five-minute molasses oatmeal breakfast recipe, and who should be careful, including people with diabetes, kidney disease or hemochromatosis.

generations. It's dark, thick, naturally
sweet, and packed with minerals that
become increasingly important as your
body ages. It's called blackstrap
molasses. Long before expensive
supplements filled pharmacy shelves,
this humble syrup was a familiar part of
everyday diets. Yet today, most people
over 60 barely give it a second thought.
In fact, back in 1951, the government
even seized copies of a best-selling
book because of what it said about this
syrup. A story I'll share with you a
little later in this video. But here's
what deserves your attention. Blackstrap
molasses contains iron, calcium,
magnesium, and potassium. Four minerals
that play important roles in maintaining
healthy bones, supporting normal muscle
function, and keeping your body working
as it should. And there's more to this
story than its nutritional content.
There's a reason this traditional food
deserves a closer look. How you use it
can make a difference, and one common
mistake could prevent you from getting
the benefits you're looking for. Near
the end, I'll also give you a simple
5-minute breakfast recipe that puts it
all to work. So before you reach for
another expensive supplement, let's take
a closer look at what a single spoonful
of this dark syrup can and cannot do for
your health after 60. Welcome to Senior
Health Board. Here, we take what the
research says about health after 60 and
put it up on the board. Plainly, slowly,
one lesson at a time. This is education,
not medical advice. So always check any
changes with your own doctor. If you'd
like more lessons like this one, please
subscribe so you don't miss the next
one. Let's begin. To understand why this
syrup is so different, you need to know
where it comes from.
When sugar is made from sugarcane, the
juice of the cane is boiled down until
sugar crystals form, and then those
crystals are spun
The syrup that's left over is boiled
again, and more sugar is taken out.
After the third boiling, almost all the
sugar that can be removed has been
removed, and what remains is a very
thick, very dark syrup. That's where the
color comes from.
The sugar has been taken away, and most
of the minerals from the cane have
stayed behind, packed into a much
smaller amount of syrup.
That's what blackstrap molasses is.
It's the same family as the lighter
molasses you might use in gingerbread
cookies, but it's the darkest,
strongest, and least sweet of them all,
with a bitter, almost smoky taste that
many people find surprising the first
time.
If you grew up in the South, you may
remember it poured over a hot biscuit or
stirred into a pot of beans. That same
jar is what we're talking about today.
The first benefit has to do with
something called antioxidants.
These are natural substances that help
protect your cells from wear and tear.
The same kind of protection you get from
berries, nuts, and dark leafy
vegetables.
In 2009, researchers at Virginia Tech
published a study in the Journal of the
American Dietetic Association.
They bought 12 natural sweeteners from
ordinary American grocery stores, along
with white sugar and corn syrup, and
measured how much antioxidant power each
one had.
White sugar had almost none at all.
Honey, maple syrup, and brown sugar
landed somewhere in the middle.
And at the very top of the list, far
ahead of everything else, were dark and
blackstrap molasses.
The researchers worked out that if
people used these darker sweeteners
instead of white sugar, they could add
about as many antioxidants to their day
as they'd get from a serving of berries
or nuts.
So, if you sweeten your oatmeal or your
tea with a little sugar every morning,
switching that sugar to a spoonful of
blackstrap is one of the easiest trades
you can make. You're still having
something sweet, but you're getting
something back from it.
I'd love to know something. Did your
mother or grandmother keep a jar of
molasses in the kitchen? Type yes or no
in the comments.
The next benefit is one that matters
more and more with every year after 60,
because it has to do with your bones.
Most people think of milk when they
think of strong bones, and calcium is
important, but bones actually need a
team of minerals to stay strong. Calcium
is the main building block. Magnesium
helps the body use that calcium
properly, and potassium helps protect
bone from slowly losing minerals over
time.
After 60, bones lose minerals faster
than the body can rebuild them. For
women, this speeds up after menopause,
and for men, it usually starts a little
later, but it happens to almost
everyone. And when there isn't enough
calcium coming in from food, the body
takes what it needs from the bones
themselves, because your heart and
muscles need calcium every second of the
day. So, the minerals you eat matter
more now than they did at 40. One
tablespoon of blackstrap molasses
contains about 15% of the calcium you
need in a day. It also has around 10% of
your daily magnesium. For a single
spoonful of something sweet, that's very
unusual. White sugar, honey, and maple
syrup have almost none of either.
Magnesium is the one many older
Americans fall short on.
National nutrition surveys in the United
States have found that a large share of
adults over 60 don't get the recommended
amount from their food. And magnesium
does far more than help your bones. It's
involved in hundreds of jobs in the
body, including turning food into
energy, and keeping muscles and nerves
working smoothly.
Hazel is 72, a retired seamstress from
Kentucky, and she's been careful about
her bones ever since her sister broke a
wrist in a fall. She drinks her milk and
takes her walks, but she never thought
about magnesium until her doctor
mentioned that her diet was low in it.
She started putting a teaspoon of
blackstrap in her morning oatmeal along
with a handful of pumpkin seeds, which
are also rich in magnesium. It's a small
change, but it's one she actually
enjoys, and that's why she's kept it up.
One thing to remember is that molasses
is a helper, not a treatment. If you
have osteoporosis, keep taking whatever
your doctor has prescribed. A spoonful
of molasses adds to a good diet, but it
doesn't replace medicine. The third
benefit surprised even the researchers
who studied it because it has to do with
blood sugar.
You'd think that anything made from
sugarcane would be bad news for blood
sugar. Blackstrap molasses does contain
sugar, about 10 g in a tablespoon, so
it's not a free food, but it behaves
differently from white sugar, and that's
because of everything else that's still
in it. In 2016, a team of researchers in
Australia published a study in the
European Journal of Nutrition. They gave
volunteers the same breakfast on
different days. The only difference was
that some breakfasts had a concentrate
made from sugarcane molasses added to
them. Their blood sugar curves looked
about the same each time, but the amount
of insulin their bodies had to release
to handle the breakfast went down, and
the more of the molasses concentrate
they had, the lower the insulin went.
The effect was strongest in people whose
bodies were already working harder to
control their blood sugar. Insulin is
the hormone that moves sugar out of your
blood and into your cells.
When your body has to release large
amounts of it after every meal, that's a
strain over time, and those big swings
are part of why people feel a burst of
energy after a sweet breakfast and then
a slump an hour or two later. To be fair
to the science, the volunteers in that
study had a special concentrate made
from molasses, not a spoonful from a
jar. So, nobody can promise that the
molasses in your kitchen will do exactly
the same thing,
but it does show that the natural
compounds in sugarcane molasses may
soften the way your body reacts to a
meal. And if you're going to have
something sweet in the morning anyway, a
little blackstrap is a much better
choice than a spoonful of white sugar.
There are easy places to make that swap.
A teaspoon in your tea instead of sugar
works well, as long as it's not the tea
you have with your main meal for a
reason you'll understand in a few
minutes. You can stir it into plain
yogurt, use it in a homemade barbecue
sauce, or a pot of baked beans, or
replace part of the brown sugar in a
muffin or cookie recipe. The taste is
strong, so a little goes a long way.
If you have diabetes, the sugar in
molasses still counts. Talk to your
doctor before adding it, and count it as
part of your carbohydrates for that
meal.
If you're still with me, type the number
three in the comments because now it's
time for the story I promised you at the
beginning.
In 1950, a nutrition writer named
Gaylord Hauser published a book called
Look Younger, Live Longer. Hauser was
famous at the time. Movie stars like
Greta Garbo and Marlene Dietrich
followed his advice, and his book was
condensed in Reader's Digest, which
meant it reached millions of American
homes. In it, he promoted five foods he
called wonder foods. They were brewer's
yeast, wheat germ, yogurt, skim milk,
and blackstrap molasses. He promised his
readers that these foods could add five
youthful years to their lives. Americans
went looking for blackstrap molasses in
grocery stores all over the country. And
in 1951, the Food and Drug
Administration seized copies of the
book. Their complaint wasn't that
molasses was dangerous.
It was that the book was being used to
help sell one particular brand of
blackstrap molasses with promises that
went far beyond what anyone could prove.
That's an important lesson, and it's
exactly the spirit of this video. Hauser
made molasses sound like a miracle, and
it isn't one. Some of the claims you'll
still find online today, that it turns
gray hair dark again, or prevents
cancer, have no real evidence behind
them. But your grandmother's spoonful
was not just a fad, either. The minerals
in it are real, and they matter more
after 60 than at almost any other time
of life. So far, you've seen three
benefits: the antioxidants, the bone
minerals, and the gentler effect on
blood sugar. The two that matter most
are still ahead. If you're finding this
useful, now is a great time to
subscribe, so you don't miss the next
lesson.
The second benefit is about your heart.
Potassium is a mineral that helps your
body balance out the salt you eat. When
you have enough potassium, your kidneys
get rid of extra salt more easily, and
the walls of your blood vessels can
relax. That's why the American Heart
Association recommends potassium-rich
foods as one of the ways to help keep
blood pressure in a healthy range. Most
Americans, at every age, eat far less
potassium than they should, and far more
salt. A tablespoon of blackstrap
molasses gives you about 10% of the
potassium you need for the day. On its
own, that won't fix high blood pressure,
but it's another small step in the right
direction, especially if it helps you
eat a bowl of oatmeal or a sweet potato
instead of a salty packaged breakfast.
Gene is 74, a retired mail sorter from
Ohio, and his blood pressure had been
creeping up for years. His doctor told
him to cut back on salt and eat more
fruit and vegetables. Gene started his
mornings with oatmeal sweetened with a
spoonful of blackstrap and a sliced
banana, instead of the bacon and toast
he'd eaten for 40 years. He likes that
it tastes a little like the gingerbread
his mother used to make at Christmas.
There's one important warning with
potassium, though. If you have kidney
disease, your kidneys may not be able to
get rid of extra potassium properly.
Some blood pressure and heart medicines
also make the body hold on to potassium,
like certain water pills and the common
pressure medicines called ACE
inhibitors. If you have kidney problems
or take any of those, ask your doctor
before adding molasses or any other
potassium-rich food every day. Tell me
in the comments, do you know what your
last blood pressure reading was? Just
the top number is fine. The number one
benefit is the reason your grandmother
took this syrup in the first place, and
it has everything to do with the
tiredness we talked about at the very
beginning.
Your blood carries oxygen to every part
of your body, and the part of your blood
that does the carrying is iron. You can
think of iron as the little trucks that
pick up oxygen in your lungs and deliver
it to your muscles and your brain. When
you don't have enough iron, there are
fewer trucks on the road. Your muscles
get less oxygen. Your brain gets less
oxygen, and you feel tired, weak, short
of breath on the stairs, and sometimes
cold all the time.
This is far more common after 60 than
most people realize.
In 2004, researchers published a large
study in the journal Blood using
national health data from the United
States. They found that about 1 in 10
Americans over 65 had anemia, which
simply means too few healthy red blood
cells. And about a third of those cases
were caused by the body not getting
enough of something it needs, mainly
iron, vitamin B12, or folate.
Tiredness isn't the only sign. Low iron
can also show up as pale skin, nails
that break easily, feeling cold when
everyone else is comfortable, restless
legs in the evening, and sometimes a
strange craving to chew ice.
There's a simple check you can do in
front of a mirror. Gently pull down your
lower eyelid and look at the inside.
It's normally a healthy pink or red. If
it looks very pale, that's worth
mentioning to your doctor. It isn't a
test, but it's a useful clue. 1 Tbsp of
blackstrap molasses has about 15 to 20%
of the iron you need in a day.
That's more than most people would ever
guess from a spoonful of syrup. This is
why old-time doctors and grandmothers
used it as a tonic for what they called
tired blood.
But there's a catch, and it's the
morning habit I mentioned at the very
beginning. The iron in molasses comes
from a plant, and plant iron is harder
for the body to absorb than the iron in
meat. Coffee and tea both contain
natural substances that latch onto this
kind of iron and stop your body from
taking it in. In some studies, a cup of
tea or coffee with a meal cut the iron
the body absorbed by more than half. So,
if you stir your spoonful of molasses
into your morning coffee, which is
exactly what a lot of people do, you may
be losing much of the iron you were
taking it for. The fix is simple. Take
your molasses at least an hour apart
from coffee or tea, and pair it with
vitamin C, which does the opposite and
helps your body absorb plant iron much
better. That's why the old tonic was
made with a squeeze of lemon.
Your grandmother may not have known the
chemistry, but she had the recipe right.
May is 69, and she'd been dragging
herself through the afternoons for
months. She already took a spoonful of
molasses stirred into her coffee because
her mother always had. When her doctor
checked her blood, her iron was low. She
moved the molasses to a glass of warm
water with lemon in the middle of the
morning, and kept her coffee for
breakfast. Along with the iron tablets
her doctor prescribed, her energy came
back over the next couple of months. Low
iron should always be checked by a
doctor because it can be a sign of
something else, like slow bleeding in
the stomach or intestines. Molasses can
support your iron, but it's not a
replacement for finding out why it's
low.
So, how do you actually use blackstrap
molasses?
First, buy the right kind. Look for a
jar or bottle that says blackstrap
molasses and unsulfured on the label.
It's usually in the baking aisle near
the syrups, and it's inexpensive.
Regular light or dark molasses has the
same taste family, but fewer minerals.
Start with 1 tsp a day for the first
week because the taste is strong, and
your stomach may need to get used to it.
If that goes well, you can move up to 1
tbsp a day. There's no reason to take
more than that. The simplest way is the
old tonic. Stir 1 Tbsp into a mug of
warm water, add a good squeeze of fresh
lemon, and drink it in the middle of the
morning, at least an hour away from your
coffee or tea. Then rinse your mouth
with plain water because molasses is
sticky and it isn't kind to your teeth
if it sits there.
Before we go on, go and have a look in
your pantry today. If there's an old jar
of molasses at the back of a shelf,
check the label and see if it says
blackstrap. Many people find they've had
it all along. And now for the small
recipe I promised you at the beginning.
It's a warm molasses breakfast bowl and
it takes about 5 minutes. Cook half a
cup of rolled oats in a cup of milk or
water. When it's done, stir in 1 tsp of
blackstrap molasses and a pinch of
cinnamon. Top it with a small handful of
pumpkin seeds or walnuts for extra
magnesium. Then have a few strawberries
or an orange on the side because the
vitamin C helps you absorb the iron from
the molasses. It tastes a bit like
gingerbread. It keeps you full until
lunch and it gives you a little of every
benefit we've talked about today. Just
keep your coffee for another time of
day. If you'd like to try it for 2
weeks, the first week is 1 tsp a day in
the oatmeal or the warm lemon water. In
the second week, if you're comfortable,
move up to a tablespoon. Notice how you
feel in the afternoons. And if you have
a blood test coming up, ask your doctor
to include your iron levels so you have
a real number to compare. If oatmeal
isn't your favorite, there are other
easy ways to get your spoonful. You can
stir it into a cup of plain yogurt with
a few slices of banana. Brush a little
over carrots or sweet potatoes before
roasting them. Or mix a teaspoon with a
bit of mustard as a glaze for chicken.
Some people even stir a small spoonful
into a mug of warm water with a slice of
fresh ginger before bed.
Whatever you choose, keep it to 1 Tbsp a
day and keep it away from your coffee
and tea. If you're going to try the warm
molasses breakfast or any of these other
ideas, type the word oats in the
comments.
Blackstrap molasses is a food, but it
isn't right for everyone. If you have
diabetes, remember that each tablespoon
has about 10 g of sugar, so it has to
fit into your daily carbohydrates. If
you have kidney disease or you take
medicines that raise potassium, check
with your doctor first. If you have a
condition called hemochromatosis, where
the body stores too much iron, you
shouldn't add iron-rich foods without
your doctor's advice. And don't let
molasses hide a real problem. Tiredness
that comes on suddenly or comes with
shortness of breath, chest pain,
dizziness, black or tarry stools, or
weight loss you can't explain needs a
doctor rather than a home remedy. A
simple blood test, usually a complete
blood count, iron levels, and vitamin
B12 can show whether something is behind
it. So, that's the black syrup your
grandmother kept in the pantry. It has
more antioxidants than honey, minerals
for your bones, a gentler effect than
white sugar, potassium for your heart,
and iron for tired blood, as long as you
keep it away from your morning coffee.
It isn't a miracle, and Gayelord Hauser
learned it the hard way in 1951, but a
single spoonful can be a small, real,
everyday help after 60. Tomorrow
morning, try 1 tsp in warm water with
lemon or in a bowl of oatmeal. Tell me
in the comments how it tasted and
whether it brought back any memories. If
you know someone over 60 who's always
tired in the afternoons, please send
them this video. And if you haven't
subscribed yet, please do so you don't
miss the next lesson. This is Senior
Health Board. One spoonful 1 hour from
your coffee, and I'll see you in the
next lesson.

records.text:
Doctor Reveals: The #1 Best Vegetable for Blood Sugar After 60
What is the best vegetable for blood sugar after 60? More than half of Americans over 65 have prediabetes, and many people with high blood sugar don’t know it. In this lesson, you’ll learn which vegetables help lower blood sugar after meals, why blood sugar gets harder to control as we age, and the simple food order trick that cut blood sugar spikes by 37 percent in a study from Weill Cornell Medicine.
We count down five vegetables for diabetes and prediabetes in seniors: okra, broccoli, beans and lentils, leafy greens, and the number one vegetable most people never buy. You’ll see how fiber slows sugar down, how sulforaphane in broccoli affects the liver, why beans can lower A1C, how magnesium in leafy greens helps insulin work, and what research shows about the vegetable at number one. You’ll also learn how to cook it so it’s easy on older teeth and stomachs.
At the end, you’ll get the Vegetable First Plan: a simple 7-day plan to lower blood sugar naturally after 60 by eating vegetables first, building a half plate of vegetables, and taking a short walk after meals.


Research referenced in this video:
Shukla AP et al. Diabetes Care, 2015: food order (vegetables and protein before carbohydrates) and blood sugar after meals
US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention: National Diabetes Statistics Report
Axelsson AS et al. Science Translational Medicine, 2017: sulforaphane from broccoli sprout extract and fasting blood sugar in type 2 diabetes
Jenkins DJ et al. Archives of Internal Medicine, 2012: legumes (beans, chickpeas, lentils) and A1C in type 2 diabetes
Carter P et al. BMJ, 2010: green leafy vegetables and risk of type 2 diabetes
National Institutes of Health, Office of Dietary Supplements: magnesium in older adults
Mongraykang J et al. Life, 2025: asparagus powder supplementation and fasting blood sugar
Hafizur RM et al. British Journal of Nutrition, 2012: asparagus extract and insulin secretion
Choi HK et al. New England Journal of Medicine, 2004: purine-rich foods and risk of gout
Markt SC et al. BMJ, 2016: genetics of smelling asparagus in urine


This video is for educational purposes only and is not medical advice. If you take insulin, diabetes medication or warfarin, or if you have kidney disease, talk to your doctor before changing your diet or any medication.

Which vegetable do you eat first at dinner? Tell us in the comments. If this lesson helped you, subscribe to Senior Health Board and share it with someone you love who’s over 60.

even chance your blood sugar is already
higher than it should be and you don't
know it. According to the CDC, more than
half of Americans over 65 have
pre-diabetes. That's about 31 million
people and among adults who already have
diabetes, more than one in four has
never been told. Most of them feel fine.
A little tired after lunch, a little
foggy in the afternoon, thirsty at
night. Things that are easy to blame on
age. The vegetable in that woman's hand
shows up on most American tables about
once a year next to the Easter ham. Last
year, researchers in Thailand gave
adults a daily dose of it, ground into a
powder for 12 weeks. Compared with
people taking a dummy pill, their
fasting blood sugar came out lower. It's
number one on today's list and by the
end, you'll know exactly how to cook it.
First though, a lunch experiment from
New York. 11 people with diabetes ate
the exact same lunch on two different
days. Grilled chicken, a salad, a slice
of bread and a small glass of orange
juice. Same plate, same amounts every
time. On one of those days, their blood
sugar an hour later was 37% lower than
on the other.
The only thing that changed was which
bite they took first. In the next few
minutes, you'll know which one and you
can try it at dinner tonight. Welcome to
Senior Health Board. Here we take what
the research says about health after 60
and put it up on the board, plainly,
slowly, one lesson at a time. Before we
start, tell me in the comments, has your
doctor ever said the word pre-diabetes
to you or is your blood sugar something
you've never really checked? I read
every answer. Let's begin.
That lunch study was run in 2015 by a
team at Weill Cornell Medicine in New
York. All 11 volunteers had type 2
diabetes and all of them took the common
diabetes pill metformin. On the first
day, they ate the bread and juice first,
then the chicken and vegetables 15
minutes later. On the second day, they
ate the same meal in the opposite order.
Vegetables and chicken first, bread and
juice last. When the vegetables and
protein came first, their blood sugar
was about 29% lower after half an hour,
37% lower after an hour, and 17% lower
after 2 hours. Their insulin levels were
lower, too. The study was published in
the journal Diabetes Care. Nothing was
taken away. Nobody counted calories. The
only thing that changed was the order.
Inside your stomach, the reason is
simple. When vegetables reach your
stomach first, their fiber forms a kind
of soft mesh. When the bread arrives a
few minutes later, it gets caught in
that mesh. The starch breaks down into
sugar more slowly, and it trickles into
your blood instead of pouring in all at
once.
Doctors who study this sometimes call it
food sequencing. You can call it
vegetables first. You can start tonight.
When you sit down to dinner, eat your
vegetables before anything else, then
the meat, fish, or eggs, then the
potato, rice, bread, or pasta last. Give
yourself 10 minutes or so between the
vegetables and the starch if you can.
Now, which vegetables work best for
this?
Some are much better at it than others,
and the one at the top of our list is
the one most people never buy. We'll
count down five vegetables, and at the
end, I'll put everything into a simple
7-day plan you can start this week.
Before we go on, tell me in the
comments, what do you usually eat first
at dinner? The meat, the potatoes, or
the vegetables? Most people have never
thought about it. Before we count down,
it helps to know why blood sugar gets
harder to control after 60 in the first
place. Think of your muscles as the
biggest sugar storage room in your body.
After a meal, insulin acts like a key.
It opens the doors of your muscle cells
and sugar moves out of your blood and
into the muscles where it's stored or
burned for energy. After 60, two things
happen to that storage room. First, it
gets smaller. Most of us lose a little
muscle every year from middle age on.
So, there's simply less room to put the
sugar.
Second, the locks get stiff. The muscle
cells respond less to insulin's key.
Doctors call this insulin resistance.
Your pancreas makes more insulin to
force the doors open. And for a while
that works, but over years it struggles
to keep up. The first place this shows
up is after meals. Your fasting number
in the morning may still look normal,
while the hour after lunch your blood
sugar shoots much higher than it used
to. Those spikes are what wear down
blood vessels, nerves, eyes, and kidneys
over time. They're also why you feel
sleepy and foggy after a big plate of
pasta. So, the goal isn't to stop
eating. The goal is to flatten the
spikes. And that's exactly what the
right vegetables do. They slow the sugar
down. They feed the good bacteria in
your gut. And some of them seem to help
the body use insulin better. If you're
still with me, tell me in the comments.
Do you ever feel sleepy or foggy an hour
after lunch? That feeling may be telling
you more than you think. Let's start the
countdown. Number five is a vegetable
people either love or can't stand, okra.
If you've ever cut into fresh okra, you
know the slippery, slightly sticky juice
inside. That slipperiness is soluble
fiber. When it meets the liquid in your
stomach, it turns into a thick gel. And
that gel slows down how fast sugar from
the rest of the meal reaches your blood,
the same way a thick milkshake drains
through a straw more slowly than water.
Okra has been studied as a blood sugar
food in several small trials, mostly in
Asia and the Middle East, and the
results have been encouraging but not
large. A cup of cooked okra has only
about 7 g of carbohydrate, and about 3
to 4 of those grams are fiber. If the
slime is what puts you off, there's a
simple fix. Cook it whole instead of
sliced, or roast it in a hot oven with a
little olive oil until the edges brown.
Roasting dries out most of the
stickiness. You can also add sliced okra
to a soup or stew, where the gel helps
thicken the broth. Okra slows the sugar
down. Our next vegetable may help your
body handle it once it gets there.
Number four is a vegetable your mother
probably made you eat, broccoli.
Broccoli and its relatives carry a
natural compound called sulforaphane. It
forms when you chop or chew the
vegetable, and it seems to affect how
the liver releases sugar into the blood.
Your liver is always putting a little
sugar into your bloodstream, especially
overnight. In people with type 2
diabetes, it often puts in too much.
That's one reason morning blood sugar
can be high even when you didn't eat
anything late. In 2017, researchers at
the University of Gothenburg in Sweden
gave 97 people with type 2 diabetes
either a concentrated broccoli sprout
extract or a dummy pill for 12 weeks.
In the people who were overweight and
whose diabetes wasn't well controlled,
fasting blood sugar dropped by about 10%
compared with the dummy pill. The study
was published in Science Translational
Medicine. That was a concentrated
extract, much stronger than a serving of
broccoli on your plate, but it shows the
compound does something real. To get the
most sulforaphane from regular broccoli,
chop it and let it sit for about 10
minutes before you cook it. Then steam
it lightly until it's bright green and
just tender. Boiling it for a long time
breaks down much of the good compound.
Leonard is 73, a retired mail sorter
from Michigan, and for years his idea of
broccoli was the gray, soft kind that
came from a can. When his doctor told
him his A1C was creeping up, his
granddaughter taught him to chop it,
weigh it, and steam it for 4 minutes. He
eats it first now, before the meat and
potatoes, three or four nights a week.
If you're still with me, tell me in the
comments, how do you like your broccoli?
Steamed, roasted, or under a blanket of
cheese? Broccoli works on the sugar your
liver releases overnight. The next food
works on the sugar from your meals, and
it surprises people because it's full of
starch. Number three surprises people
because beans have starch in them. Beans
and lentils. Yes, they contain
carbohydrates, but they're packed so
tightly with fiber and protein that the
sugar comes out very slowly. Doctors say
they have a low glycemic index, which
simply means they raise blood sugar
gently instead of all at once.
In 2012, Dr. David Jenkins and his team
at the University of Toronto followed
121 people with type 2 diabetes for 3
months. One group added at least one cup
of beans, chickpeas, or lentils to their
day. The other group ate more whole
wheat foods instead. The bean group's
A1C, the 3-month average of blood sugar,
dropped by half a percentage point. The
wheat group's dropped by less. And the
bean group's blood pressure came down by
about 4.5 points as well. The study was
published in the Archives of Internal
Medicine. Half a point of A1C may sound
small. For many people, it's about what
you'd hope to see from adding a
medicine. Clyde is 76, a retired bus
mechanic from Ohio, and his lunch for 20
years was a sandwich on white bread with
a bag of chips. His dietitian didn't
take the sandwich away. She asked him to
add a cup of lentil soup before it. The
soup filled him up, so he started
leaving the chips in the cupboard. Four
months later, his A1C was down from 6.4
to 5.9.
If beans give you gas, start with a
quarter cup a day and build up slowly
over two or three weeks. Tell me in the
comments, what's your favorite way to
eat beans? Chili, soup, or straight from
the can? Somebody watching might need a
new idea. Beans slow the sugar down with
fiber and protein. The next vegetable
barely has any sugar to slow down at
all, and it carries a mineral that helps
insulin do its job. Now, naturally, my
partner Nellie, number two is a whole
family of vegetables.
Spinach, kale, collard greens, Swiss
chard, romaine, and the rest of the dark
leafy greens. They have almost no
carbohydrate at all. A big plate of raw
spinach barely moves blood sugar, and
they're full of magnesium, a mineral
your body uses to help insulin do its
job. Many older adults don't get enough
magnesium from their food.
In 2010, researchers at the University
of Leicester in England combined six
large studies with more than 220,000
people.
People who ate a little more than one
extra serving of green leafy vegetables
a day had about a 14% lower risk of
developing type 2 diabetes. The study
was published in the BMJ. Those were
studies that watched people over time,
so they can't prove the greens did it
alone, but leafy greens keep showing up
on the right side of almost every study
of diet and blood sugar.
The easiest way to use them is as the
first course, a small bowl of salad
before dinner. One important note, leafy
greens are rich in vitamin K, which
helps your blood clot. If you take the
blood thinner warfarin, you don't have
to avoid them, but your doctor will want
you to eat about the same amount each
week, so your dose stays right. Talk to
your doctor before making a big change.
Still here? Tell me in the comments
which green do you actually eat at least
once a week.
Magnesium helps insulin open the door to
your muscles, but it only works once the
sugar is already in your blood. The
vegetable at number one works one step
earlier in a place most people never
think about when it comes to blood
sugar. It's the one in her hand. Number
one is asparagus.
Most people think of it as a fancy
vegetable, something served at Easter
dinner or in a restaurant. It's actually
one of the easiest vegetables you can
cook and it's in the grocery store all
year.
It sits at the top of our list for four
reasons. First, it's almost nothing but
fiber and water. About six spears, a
typical serving, have only around 20
calories and about 4 g of carbohydrate
and half of that is fiber. You can eat a
big pile of it and your blood sugar will
barely notice. Second, asparagus carries
a special kind of fiber called inulin.
Your body can't digest inulin. Instead,
it travels to your large intestine and
feeds the good bacteria that live there.
When those bacteria feed, they make
substances that help keep the gut lining
healthy and seem to help the body handle
sugar better.
A healthier gut is one more thing
working in your favor.
Third, scientists have started testing
asparagus in people. In 2025,
researchers at Burapha University in
Thailand gave adults either a daily
capsule of asparagus powder or a dummy
pill for 12 weeks.
At the end, the asparagus group had
lower fasting blood sugar and after a
sugar drink, their blood sugar rose less
than in the dummy pill group. The study
was published in the journal Life.
Earlier work in animals points the same
way. In 2012, researchers at the
University of Karachi found that
asparagus extract helped the pancreas
release more insulin. And fourth, and
this is the reason it's number one,
asparagus is the easiest swap on the
whole list. It replaces the starchy side
dish. Instead of a scoop of mashed
potatoes or a pile of rice next to your
chicken or fish, you put six or eight
spears of asparagus.
Same plate, same meal, far less sugar.
You may have heard two worries about
asparagus. The first is gout. Asparagus
has some purines, the compounds that can
raise uric acid.
But in a large Harvard study of more
than 47,000 men, published in the New
England Journal of Medicine in 2004,
purine-rich vegetables, asparagus among
them, were not linked to a higher risk
of gout. Meat and seafood were. If you
have gout, ask your doctor, but
asparagus usually isn't the problem. The
second worry is the smell. Yes,
asparagus can make your urine smell
strange an hour or two later. That's
harmless. A 2016 study of about 6,900
people, published in the BMJ, found that
58% of men and 62% of women couldn't
smell it at all. Their noses simply
don't pick it up. Dolores is 71, a
retired church organist from
Pennsylvania. At her last checkup, her
doctor said her A1C was 6.2, in the
pre-diabetes range, and told her to cut
back on starches. She didn't want to
give up her Sunday chicken dinner, so
she made one change. The mashed potatoes
became a smaller scoop, and next to them
she put a handful of roasted asparagus,
which she ate first. Within a few weeks,
she noticed she wasn't falling asleep in
her chair after dinner anymore. Six
months later, her A1C was 5.8. If you're
still watching, tell me in the comments,
have you ever cooked asparagus at home,
or is it something you've only had in a
restaurant? Asparagus is simple, but a
few tricks make it much easier on older
teeth and stomachs. Start with the ends.
Hold a spear near the bottom and bend it
gently. It will snap right where the
tough, woody part ends. If your spears
are thick, or if you wear dentures, peel
the bottom half of each spear with a
vegetable peeler. That takes away the
stringy outer skin, and the spear
becomes tender all the way through. The
easiest way to cook it is roasting. Heat
the oven to 425°.
Lay the spears on a baking sheet,
drizzle a little olive oil, add a pinch
of salt and pepper, and roast for about
8 to 12 minutes until the tips are a
little crispy. A squeeze of lemon at the
end makes it taste bright. If you'd
rather steam it, 3 to 5 minutes is
enough. It should be bright green and
bend a little when you lift it. Gray and
floppy means it's overcooked. Frozen
asparagus works fine, too, and it's
often cheaper. And to keep fresh
asparagus from drying out, stand the
bunch upright in a glass with an inch of
water in the bottom, like flowers, and
keep it in the refrigerator. It stays
fresh for several days that way.
Let's put it all together into a simple
plan you can start this week. I call it
the vegetable first plan. Step one is
the order. At lunch and dinner, eat your
vegetables first, then your protein,
then your starch last. That's the 37%
trick from the beginning, and it works
with any vegetable on this list.
Step two is the half plate. Fill half
your plate with non-starchy vegetables,
like asparagus, broccoli, leafy greens,
or okra. A quarter of the plate goes to
protein, and a quarter to starch. If
you've always had potatoes taking up
half the plate, this one change does a
lot of work. Step three is the swap. At
least three nights a week, let asparagus
or another green vegetable take the
place of the potato, rice, or bread on
the side.
You don't have to give them up. Just
make the scoop smaller, and let the
green vegetable fill the space. Step
four is the cup of beans.
Most days, add about 1 cup of beans,
lentils, or chickpeas somewhere in your
meals. In a soup, in a salad, in chili,
or on the side. Start with less if
you're not used to them. Step five is
the walk. After your biggest meal, take
a slow 10-minute walk, even if it's just
around the house or up and down the
driveway. Your muscles pull sugar out of
your blood when they move. So, the walk
and the vegetables work together. For
your first week, change the order at
dinner on day one. On days two and
three, swap half your starch for
asparagus. On days four and five, add
beans at lunch. On days six and seven,
put it all together and add the walk. If
you have a glucose meter, check 1 hour
after dinner on day one and again on day
seven. Many people are surprised by the
difference.
For most people, more vegetables are
only good news. But, a few situations
need a conversation with your doctor
first. If you take insulin or certain
diabetes pills that push your blood
sugar down, a big change in how you eat
can sometimes drop it too low. Signs of
low blood sugar include shakiness,
sweating, sudden hunger, confusion, or a
racing heart. Talk to your doctor before
changing any medication and let them
know if you're changing how you eat. If
you take warfarin, keep your leafy
greens and asparagus about the same from
week to week and tell your doctor about
the change. If you have kidney disease,
ask before adding a lot of spinach,
beans, or other high potassium foods.
And if you're not used to much fiber,
add these vegetables a little at a time
and drink more water as you go.
A sudden jump in fiber can cause
bloating or gas for a week or two while
your gut adjusts.
And if you've never had your blood sugar
checked, ask for an A1C test at your
next visit. It's a simple blood test and
it tells you where you stand. So, the
next time you're in the the store, slow
down in the produce aisle and pick up a
bunch of asparagus. Snap the ends, roast
it with a little olive oil, and eat it
first. Tell me in the comments which
change you'll try first, the order, the
half plate, or the asparagus swap. And
if someone you love has been told their
blood sugar is creeping up, send them
this lesson. It might be the easiest
change they ever make. Subscribe so you
don't miss the next lesson. This is
Senior Health Board, vegetables first,
and I'll see you in the next lesson.

records.text:
Stool STUCK in the Rectum! What Is It and What to Do After 60

Stool stuck in the rectum? Feeling full and heavy at the bottom, but nothing will come out no matter how hard you push? After 60, that hard push on the toilet can do more than you think. In this lesson, we explain what happens inside your body when stool gets stuck, why straining doesn't move a hard lump, and what that push does to your heart and blood pressure, especially first thing in the morning.

You'll learn what a fecal impaction is, why constipation gets worse with age, which common medications slow the bowels, and why your thirst signal gets weaker after 60. We also cover the "diarrhea trap": why watery leaking after days of constipation can actually be a sign of a blockage, and why taking anti-diarrhea medicine in that situation can make things much worse.

Then we go step by step through what to do when stool feels stuck right now, the simple morning routine that helps your body go on its own, the toilet position that makes it easier, and the warning signs that mean you should go to the emergency room.

Research referenced in this video:
Phillips PA et al. New England Journal of Medicine, 1984 – reduced thirst after water deprivation in healthy older men
Rey E et al. PLOS ONE, 2014 – nationwide study of constipation and fecal impaction in 34 Spanish nursing homes
Attaluri A et al. Alimentary Pharmacology & Therapeutics, 2011 – prunes vs. psyllium for constipation
Modi RM et al. Journal of Clinical Gastroenterology, 2019 – footstool (defecation posture device) and straining
Clinical literature on defecation syncope and the Valsalva maneuver

This video is for education only, not medical advice. Always check any changes with your own doctor.

Which change are you going to start with tomorrow morning? Tell us in the comments. If this lesson helped you, subscribe to Senior Health Board and share it with someone you love who's over 60.

#constipation #seniorhealth #over60 #guthealth #healthyaging

It feels like the most ordinary thing in
the world. Everybody does it. And when
stool feels stuck, pushing harder seems
like the only answer anybody has. But,
doctors who look after older adults see
what that push can lead to. They see
people who fainted on the bathroom floor
at 6:00 in the morning. They see people
who spent 3 days treating what looked
like diarrhea when the real problem was
the exact opposite. And they see people
who have struggled for years without

habit was keeping them stuck. And one
part of this will sound odd at first.
The step that helps the most doesn't
happen in the bathroom at all. It
happens in your kitchen about half an
hour earlier, and it takes less effort
than making your bed. By the end of this
lesson, you'll know exactly what it is
and why your body has been waiting for
it every single morning. Welcome to
Senior Health Board. Here, we take what
the research says about health after 60
and put it up on the board, plainly,
slowly, one lesson at a time. Let's
begin with a man named Harold. Harold is
78, a retired bus driver from Michigan.
He has been an early riser his whole
life, and his mornings run like a
timetable. He wakes up at a quarter to
6:00, swallows his blood pressure pill
and his iron tablet with a sip of water,
and heads straight for the bathroom.
For about a week, things hadn't been
moving well. He'd go in, sit, wait, and
come out with nothing. He felt heavy and
full low in his belly, as though
something was sitting right at the exit
and refused to leave.
So, that Tuesday morning, he decided he
going to settle it. He sat down, took a
big breath, held it, and pushed as hard
as he could. Then, he did it again.
On the third push, the room tilted. His
ears started ringing. The edges of his

remembered was reaching for the towel
rail.
We'll come back to Harold and what his
wife found when she opened that door.
But first, you need to understand what
was happening inside him because the
same thing happens in millions of
bathrooms every morning, usually without
anyone fainting, and usually without
anyone knowing.
Let's start with where stool comes from
and why it gets stuck.
Your large intestine, the colon, is a
muscular tube about 5 ft long. It has
two jobs. The first is to keep moving
waste toward the exit with slow rolling
squeezes, a little like the way you push
toothpaste along a tube.
The second is to pull water back out of
that waste so your body doesn't lose it.
At the very end, sits the rectum. You
can think of it as a waiting room. Stool
arrives there, the walls stretch, and
that stretch sends a message to your
brain that says, "It's time."
Below the waiting room is a door, a ring
of muscle that stays closed until you
decide to open it. When everything works
on schedule, stool arrives in the
waiting room soft and goes out the door
soon after.
The trouble begins when stool waits too
long.
The colon never stops pulling out water.
So the longer stool sits, the drier it
gets. One day becomes two, two becomes
four, and something that started out
soft slowly turns into a hard, dry lump,
like clay left out in the sun.
Doctors call this a fecal impaction.
It's stool that has become so hard and
so large that the body can't push it out
on its own.
And this is where the push comes in.
When you strain against a lump that
hard, you're pushing against something
that doesn't give. The lump barely
moves. But the pressure you create has
to go somewhere, and it goes straight
into your chest. When you take a deep
breath, close your throat, and bear
down, doctors call that the Valsalva
maneuver. It's named after an Italian
anatomist who described it more than 300
years ago. And it's the same thing you
do when you lift something heavy or blow
up a stiff balloon. During that push,
the pressure inside your chest rises
sharply. That pressure squeezes the
large veins that carry blood back into
your heart. Less blood comes back in, so
less blood goes out. Your blood pressure
jumps for a moment and then drops, and
your brain briefly gets less blood than
it wants. Then, as you let your breath
go, everything rushes back the other
way.
At the same time, the strain can trigger
a nerve reflex that slows the heartbeat.
A young, flexible heart and set of blood
vessels handle all of this without
anyone noticing. After 60, the system is
slower to adjust. Arteries are stiffer.
Many people are taking pills that lower
blood pressure or slow the heart.
And the push often happens first thing
in the morning, minutes after getting
out of bed, before the body has fully
woken up. Put all of that together, and
you can see what happened to Harold. He
had a blood pressure pill working in his
body. He had just stood up from a night
of lying flat, and then he pushed hard
three times in a row. Doctors have a
name for fainting this way. They call it
defecation syncope, which simply means
passing out during or after a movement.
It isn't common, but it shows up more
often in older adults, and it usually
happens when someone gets up from bed
and then strains. The faint itself is
short. The fall is the dangerous part
because a bathroom is full of hard
edges, a tub, a sink, and a tile floor.
For someone with heart disease,
straining is also one of the things
cardiologists ask patients to avoid
because of the stress that push puts on
the heart. So, that's the first question
answered. Pushing harder doesn't move a
hard lump, and it does put a real load
on your heart.
The next question is why this happens so
much more often after 60. And part of
the answer is in your medicine cabinet.
There are four main reasons stool gets
stuck more often with age, and most
people have at least two of them. The
first is thirst. In 1984, researchers
published a study in the New England
Journal of Medicine comparing healthy
men in their late 60s and early 70s with
men in their 20s. Both groups went 24
hours without water. Afterward, the
older men felt less thirsty and drank
less, even though their bodies needed
the water just as much. That finding has
been repeated many times since. After
60, your thirst alarm gets quieter. And
when you're even a little short on
water, your colon takes more of it out
of your stool.
Let's make this personal for a second.
Think about yesterday. Count the glasses
of water you actually drank, not the
ones you meant to drink. For a lot of
people over 70, the honest number is
three or four.
The second reason is medication. Many of
the most common pills taken after 60
slow the bowels as a side effect. That
list includes strong pain relievers,
iron tablets, calcium supplements, some
blood pressure pills, many allergy and
sleep medicines, and some
antidepressants.
One of them alone might not cause
trouble. Two or three together often do.
Harold was taking an iron tablet every
morning, and nobody had ever connected
it to his bathroom troubles.
>> [snorts]
>> If you think one of your medicines might
be slowing you down, talk to your doctor
before changing any medication. There's
often a simple adjustment. The third
reason is the colon itself. With age,
those rolling squeezes that move stool
along tend to become slower and weaker.
Less walking and more sitting slow them
down even more because movement of the
body helps move the bowel.
The fourth reason is a habit, and it
might surprise you.
Many people raised in an earlier
generation learned to hold it in. Not at
work, not in a public restroom, not at
someone else's house, not now.
Over the years, ignoring the urge
teaches the waiting room to stop sending
the message. The stretch signal gets
weaker, stool waits longer, and every
extra hour of waiting means drier,
harder stool.
How common does this get? In Spain,
researchers studied residents of 34
nursing homes across the country, and
the results were published in 2014 in
the journal PLOS ONE.
About seven in 10 residents had chronic
constipation. And among those with
chronic constipation, nearly half had
experienced a fecal impaction. If you've
been dealing with any of this, tell me
in the comments which of those four
reasons sounds the most like you.
You'd be surprised how many people
watching are in the same spot. And there
are a few ideas that keep people stuck
even when they're trying to do
everything right. Let's clear those up

have to go every day. You don't. Doctors
usually describe a normal range as
anywhere from three times a day to three
times a week.
What matters is what's normal for you
and whether it has changed. If you've
gone every other day for 40 years,
that's your rhythm.
The warning sign is a change or stool
that has become hard and painful to
pass.
The second is that prunes are just an
old wives' tale.
They're actually one of the few home
remedies with research behind them.
In a small study published in 2011,
adults with constipation who ate prunes

fiber powder.
Prunes carry fiber and a natural sugar
alcohol called sorbitol, which pulls
water into the bowel. A small handful a
day is an easy place to start.
The third is that more fiber always
helps.

short on water or when a hard lump is
already stuck, you can end up with more
of a traffic jam. Water first, then
fiber, slowly.

whole lesson and it's the one that sends

Dorothy is 74, a retired church
secretary from Georgia.
She'd been constipated for most of a
week and then, on Saturday morning,

stool. Not much, but it came without
warning and it kept coming in small
amounts all day long.
To Dorothy, the answer seemed obvious.
She had diarrhea.
So, she did what most of us would do.
She went to the pharmacy, bought an
anti-diarrhea medicine and took it as
the box directed for 3 days.
By Tuesday, she was in the emergency
room with a swollen, painful belly and a
hard lump that had to be removed by a
doctor.
What happened to Dorothy has a name.
Doctors call it overflow.
When a hard lump is stuck in the rectum,
the bowel above it doesn't stop working.
Liquid stool keeps arriving from higher
up. It can't get past the lump, so it
seeps around the edges and leaks out.
From the outside, it looks exactly like
diarrhea.
In reality, it's a sign of a blockage.
Anti-diarrhea medicine works by slowing
the bowel down. Normally, that's what
you want. But when the problem is a
blockage, slowing the bowel takes away
the one thing still trying to move
things along.
That's how a stuck lump that could have
been handled at home turns into an
emergency. So, that's the second
question answered. If you've been
constipated for several days and then
suddenly start leaking watery stool,
don't reach for diarrhea medicine. Call
your doctor first and tell them about
both, the days of constipation and the
leaking. That combination is the clue.
If you're still with me, tell me in the
comments whether you'd ever heard of
overflow before today. Most people
haven't, and it's one of the most useful
things you can pass on to a friend.
Let's say you're in that situation
today. You feel full and heavy at the
bottom. You've sat on the toilet more
than once with no result, and it's been
several days. These are the safe steps.
First, stop pushing. I know your body is
telling you to push harder, but pushing
won't move a hard lump, and you now know
what it does to your heart. Breathe out
slowly while you sit. Never hold your
breath and bear down. Second, use
something that softens from below. A
pharmacy sells glycerin suppositories
and small saline enemas without a
prescription.
They work by drawing water into the hard
stool and making the passage slippery.
Use them exactly as the package directs.
Lying on your left side for these makes
sense because of the way the lower bowel
curves. And give it time. Many people
rush to the toilet after 5 minutes and
lose the benefit. Third, get up and
walk. 15 or 20 minutes of gentle walking
around the house helps wake up the
bowel. And it often does more than
sitting and waiting. Fourth, drink a
full glass of warm water or a cup of
warm tea. Warm liquid can help get the
bowel moving. And you've probably been a
little low on fluids for days. And if
none of that works within a day, or if
you have any of the warning signs I'll
give you before we finish, call your
doctor or go to urgent care.
Doctors deal with stuck stool all the
time. They have stronger enemas and if
needed, they can break up and remove the
lump themselves. It's a routine
procedure and people describe the relief
as enormous. There's nothing
embarrassing about it and waiting only
makes it harder. Now for the third
question, the habit that keeps all of
this coming back. Most people think of
the bathroom as something you do when
you feel the urge and then you push
until something happens. That's the
mistake. It's two habits really. Waiting
for an urge that has grown weak over the
years and then forcing it.
Your body has a built-in schedule you
can use instead.
When food lands in your stomach, it
sends a signal down to your colon to
start moving. Doctors call it a
gastrocolic reflex. It's strongest in
the morning, in the first half hour or
so after breakfast. That's your window.
So the routine looks like this.
Eat breakfast. Drink something warm with
it. Then, within about 20 or 30 minutes,
sit on the toilet. Even if you don't
feel much of an urge. Give it 5 to 10
minutes. Breathe slowly. Don't push.
If nothing happens, get up and try again
tomorrow at the same time.
Over a few weeks, your body starts to
expect it, and the waiting room starts
sending its message again.
How you sit matters, too.
A toilet puts your hips at a right
angle. In that position, a muscle that
wraps around the end of the bowel keeps
it bent, like a garden hose with a kink
in it.
That kink is useful when you want to
hold it in. It's a problem when you want
to let it out.
Raising your knees above your hips
relaxes that muscle and straightens the
hose. You can do that with a small
footstool, about 7 to 9 inches high.
In 2019, researchers published a study
in the Journal of Clinical
Gastroenterology of 52 volunteers who
kept a record of their bowel movements,
first without a footstool, and then with
one.
>> [snorts]
>> With the stool under their feet, they
finished faster, strained less, and felt
more completely empty afterward.
That study was done in younger adults,
but the anatomy is the same at 75.
Lean forward a little, rest your elbows
on your knees, and let your belly relax.
The rest of the plan is simple and
steady.
Drink on a schedule, not on thirst. A
full glass at breakfast, mid-morning,
lunch, mid-afternoon, and dinner covers
most people well.
Add fiber slowly from oatmeal, beans,
lentils, pears, prunes, and cooked
vegetables.
If you add it too fast, you get gas and
bloating, and you quit.
Walk most days.
And when the urge does come, answer it.
Don't put it off.
One more thing about laxatives.
Stimulant laxatives work fast, and
that's why people keep reaching for
them. But using them every day for
months can leave the bowel dependent on
them. If you find you need help more
than once in a while, ask your doctor
about gentler options that work with
your body, like stool softeners or fiber
products. So, let's go back to Harold on
the bathroom floor that Tuesday morning.
His wife, Jean, heard the thump from the
kitchen.
By the time she got the door open, he
was already coming around, pale and
sweaty, with a cut above his eyebrow
from the edge of the sink. She called
911. At the hospital, the doctors
checked his heart first. There was no
heart attack.
What they found was a man who had stood
up from bed, taken his blood pressure
pill, and then pushed hard three times
against a stool that had been building
up for a week.
His iron tablet had been slowing him
down for months. They cleared the
blockage, stitched his eyebrow, and sent
him home.
Then, his doctor sat down with him and
went through the whole picture.
They talked about the iron tablet and
the timing of his blood pressure pill.
And Harold got a new morning routine.
Water and breakfast first. The bathroom
after breakfast, not before.
A little wooden footstool his grandson
made him in shop class.
Slow breathing, no pushing.
And a walk around the block with Jean
every morning, which he says is the best
part. Jean made two more changes. She
had a grab bar put in next to the
toilet, and Harold no longer locks the
bathroom door in the morning, so she can
get in quickly if she ever needs to.
Small things, but in a bathroom full of
hard edges, they matter. Harold hasn't
fallen since. And he says his mornings
are a lot calmer now than when he was
fighting with that bathroom every day.
Before we finish, here are the signs
that mean you shouldn't wait at home.
Get medical help right away if you have
severe belly pain or a hard swollen
belly. If you're vomiting and can't keep
anything down. If you can't pass gas at
all. If you see a lot of blood or black
tarry stool. If you have a fever with
belly pain. If you suddenly can't pass
urine or you feel confused, faint or
short of breath. And if you faint on the
toilet even once tell your doctor even
if you feel fine afterward. So the next
time you sit down and nothing comes,
remember Harold. Breathe out, don't push
and give your body the routine it's been
missing. Tell me in the comments which
change you're going to start with
tomorrow morning. And if you know
someone who's been struggling with this
and keeping it to themselves, send them
this lesson. It's the kind of thing
people rarely ask about out loud. This
is Senior Health Board. Breathe out,
don't push and I'll see you in the next
lesson.

records.text:
The Hand Tremor Sign Doctors Check Before Memory Loss After 60

Shaky hands after 60: is hand tremor a sign of dementia? This video explains what the research says about essential tremor, Parkinson's disease, medicines that cause tremor, and memory changes, including where the studies disagree.

If your hands shake when you hold a cup, sign your name or rest in your lap, you will learn what doctors look at first (the Three Clues), how common essential tremor is, what can make hands shake, and a simple five-step plan to bring to your next appointment.

WHAT YOU WILL LEARN
Essential tremor vs Parkinson's tremor: shaking during movement versus shaking at rest
Why shaky hands do not always point to the brain, and which medicines, thyroid problems, caffeine and stress can turn the shake up
What large studies found about essential tremor and dementia, and why the results are mixed
Why new memory or thinking changes are worth writing down and mentioning to your doctor

YOUR FIVE-STEP PLAN
1. Record two 15-second phone videos: hands resting in your lap, then holding a full cup of water.
2. Write a one-page tremor note and list every medicine, inhaler and supplement you take.
3. Write down three memory or thinking changes from the last six months.
4. Try simple daily-life changes for two weeks.
5. Know the stroke warning signs, and call 911 right away if they appear.
Never stop or change a medicine on your own. Talk to your doctor or pharmacist first.

QUESTIONS TO ASK YOUR DOCTOR
1. What kind of tremor do I have, and how did you decide?
2. Could any of my medicines be adding to it?
3. Since I have a tremor, should we also check my memory and thinking?

RESEARCH AND SOURCES
Essential tremor and dementia, 222 adults, average age 79: Louis and colleagues, Annals of Neurology, 2024
Essential tremor and dementia, Mayo Clinic Arizona study: American Academy of Neurology annual meeting, 2024
Essential tremor and dementia in northern Manhattan: Thawani, Schupf and Louis, Neurology, 2009
Cognitive decline before essential tremor is diagnosed: Benito-Leon and colleagues, Neurology, 2013
How common is essential tremor: Louis and McCreary, 2021 review; Louis and Ottman, 2014
Essential tremor and its look-alikes: Thenganatt and Louis, Columbia University, 2012 review
Action tremor vs rest tremor: Penn Medicine, essential tremor diagnosis
Causes of tremor and everyday tips: MedlinePlus, National Library of Medicine
Caffeine and tremor: Koller and colleagues, Neurology, 1987
Albuterol prescribing information, FDA label
Stroke warning signs: American Stroke Association and University of Michigan Health

This video is for education only and is not medical advice. Always talk to your own doctor or pharmacist before changing anything. If you think you or someone near you may be having a stroke, call 911 right away.

Next week: what your handwriting and a simple spiral can show a neurologist. Subscribe to Senior Health Board for plain-English summaries of medical research for adults over 60.

#HandTremor #EssentialTremor #SeniorHealth

cabinet often don't fit. That's not

fault. So, bring the answers with you
and bring three questions. Question one,
what kind of tremor do I have and how
did you decide? Question two, could any
of my medicines be adding to it?
Question three, since I have a tremor,
should we also check my memory and
thinking? A good doctor will welcome
every one of them. And if the answer is
it's probably nothing, ask what makes
them sure. None of these questions
diagnoses anything. They just make sure
nothing important gets missed. Asking
them doesn't make you a difficult
patient. Three weeks later, Walter sat
in a doctor's office with two phone

list of memory changes. He didn't walk
out with a final answer. He walked out

drove home, picked up a screwdriver, and

one thing from today, just one. Maybe

get wrong. This is Senior Health Board.

THAT Sleeping Position Increases STROKE Risk Overnight!

If you're over 60 and you sleep flat on your back, snore, or jump out of bed in the morning, this lesson is for you. Sleeping flat on your back can make sleep apnea worse, and sleep apnea causes repeated drops in oxygen and spikes in blood pressure all night long. Research has linked sleep apnea to about twice the risk of stroke or death, and most people who have it have never been diagnosed.

In this video, we put it all up on the board: how your airway works like a soft garden hose, why gravity matters so much at night, and the 5 most common nighttime mistakes people over 60 make, from treating snoring as harmless, to the evening nightcap, to sleeping too long, to getting out of bed too fast (the "Gravity Gap"), to the #1 mistake almost everyone makes.

Then you'll learn the Safe Night Plan: how to switch to side sleeping (including the tennis ball technique), how to raise your upper body the right way, the 3-step Slow Rise for getting out of bed safely, when to ask for a sleep test, and a simple 7-day plan to get started. We also cover the BE FAST stroke warning signs so you know when to call 911.

Research referenced in this video:
Yaggi HK et al. Obstructive sleep apnea as a risk factor for stroke and death. New England Journal of Medicine, 2005.
American Academy of Sleep Medicine – estimates on undiagnosed obstructive sleep apnea.
Simou E et al. Alcohol and the risk of sleep apnoea: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Sleep Medicine, 2018.
Leng Y et al. Sleep duration and risk of fatal and nonfatal stroke. Neurology, 2015.
Saedon NI et al. The prevalence of orthostatic hypotension: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Journals of Gerontology, 2020.
Mol A et al. Orthostatic hypotension and falls in older adults. Journal of the American Medical Directors Association, 2019.

Bignold JJ et al. Poor long-term patient compliance with the tennis ball technique. Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine, 2009.
Souza FJFB et al. The influence of head-of-bed elevation in patients with obstructive sleep apnea. Sleep and Breathing, 2017.

Disclaimer: This is education, not medical advice — always check any changes with your own doctor. Talk to your doctor before changing any medication. If you notice signs of a stroke, call 911 right away.

It's 2:47 in the morning. The house is
dark and quiet. You've been asleep on
your back, the way you've slept for 40
years, flat, arms at your sides, head on
one thin pillow.
You don't remember it, but for the last
hour your breathing has been stopping.
10 seconds, 20,
then a snort, a gasp, and it starts
again.
Your spouse heard it. Maybe they nudged
you. Maybe they moved to the guest room
a while ago and never said exactly why.
Then you wake up needing the bathroom.
You sit up fast, swing your legs out,
and stand. For a moment the room tilts,

records.text:
Olive Oil Shock: What It REALLY Does to Your Arteries After 60

You pour olive oil because someone told you it was good for your heart. But what actually happens after that spoonful leaves your plate? In this lesson, we follow one spoonful of olive oil through your body, from the peppery sting in your throat to the inner lining of your arteries, and explain what the research really shows about olive oil, cholesterol and heart health after 60.

You'll learn why fresh extra virgin olive oil makes some people cough, what oleocanthal is, how olive oil affects the lining of your arteries (the endothelium), and how it helps protect LDL cholesterol from the kind of damage that builds plaque. We also cover what olive oil can't do: it doesn't dissolve plaque, unclog arteries or replace your heart medicine.

Then we go into the kitchen: the most common olive oil mistakes seniors make, like adding it on top of butter, keeping the bottle next to the stove, buying clear bottles and giant jugs, and believing "light" olive oil has fewer calories. You'll also learn how much olive oil to use per day, how to choose a good bottle, the simple throat test, and why you can safely cook with extra virgin olive oil.

Research referenced in this video:
Beauchamp GK et al. Nature, 2005 – oleocanthal and its ibuprofen-like activity in extra virgin olive oil
Yubero-Serrano EM et al. PLOS Medicine, 2020 – CORDIOPREV study, Mediterranean diet and artery function in 805 people with heart disease
Covas MI et al. Annals of Internal Medicine, 2006 – EUROLIVE study, olive oil polyphenols, HDL and oxidized LDL
Estruch R et al. New England Journal of Medicine, 2018 – PREDIMED, Mediterranean diet with extra virgin olive oil in 7,447 adults
Guasch-Ferré M et al. Journal of the American College of Cardiology, 2020 – olive oil intake and heart disease in more than 93,000 US adults
US Food and Drug Administration – qualified health claim for olive oil and coronary heart disease

This video is for education only, not medical advice. Always check any changes with your own doctor.

Which swap are you going to make first? Tell us in the comments. If this lesson helped you, subscribe to Senior Health Board and share it with someone you love who's over 60.

#oliveoil #hearthealth #seniorhealth #over60 #healthyaging
