slides down into your stomach, and for a
while, not much happens.
Oil and water don't mix, so the oil
mostly floats on top waiting its turn.
The real work starts in the small
intestine.
Your gallbladder has been holding a
supply of bile from your liver, and now
it squeezes some out.
Bile works a lot like dish soap in a
greasy frying pan. It breaks that big
pool of oil into thousands of tiny
droplets, which gives your digestive
enzymes far more surface to work on.
Then, the enzymes go to work like little
pairs of scissors snipping the fat into
smaller pieces.
Those pieces are carried to the wall of
your intestine and pulled inside.
And then, your body does something
clever. It puts the fat back together
again and packs it into small delivery
parcels wrapped in protein, so the fat
can travel through your watery blood
without clumping.
Doctors call those parcels chylomicrons.
You don't need to remember the word.
Just think of them as parcels. This is
where olive oil and butter start to go
their separate ways.
Most of the fat in olive oil is a kind
called monounsaturated fat, and the main
one has the name oleic acid. Butter,
cheese, and fatty red meat carry mostly
saturated fat. Your body packs them into
the same kind of parcels, but they don't
behave the same way once they arrive,
and the difference shows up later in
your blood and in your arteries.
Something else rides along in those
parcels. Vitamin E, the color pigments
in tomatoes and carrots, and the
protective compounds in leafy greens all
dissolve in fat. Your body absorbs much
more of them when there's some fat in
the same meal.
A salad with no dressing at all looks
healthy, but you'll take in less of
what's in it than you would from the
same salad with a spoonful of olive oil
on top. An hour or two after your meal,
the parcels reach your bloodstream, and
from there they travel past the most
important surface in this whole story.
Every artery in your body is lined on
the inside with a single thin layer of
cells. Doctors call it the endothelium.
It's thinner than a sheet of tissue
paper, and it's alive. You can think of
it as the skin on the inside of your
pipes. Every heartbeat pushes blood
across it, and it doesn't simply sit
there. It responds. When your body needs
more blood, when you climb a flight of
stairs or carry the groceries in from
the car, that lining releases a gas
called nitric oxide. Nitric oxide tells
the thin band of muscle around the
artery to relax. The artery opens wider,
and blood flows through more easily.
After 60, this lining tends to get
lazier. Studies that measure how well
arteries widen show a slow decline from
middle age onward, and it drops faster
in people with high blood pressure,
diabetes, high cholesterol, or a history
of smoking. A lazy lining means stiffer
arteries and higher pressure. It's also
the place where plaque gets its start.
Years before a scan would ever show a
blockage, the lining has usually stopped
doing its job well. Doctors can measure
this with an ultrasound of the arm.
They tighten a blood pressure cuff for
about 5 minutes, let it go, and watch
how much the main artery widens as the
blood rushes back in. A healthy lining
opens wide. A tired one barely moves.
This is one of the places where olive
oil keeps turning up in the research. In
several small trials, volunteers had
their arteries checked a few hours after
a meal.
When the meal was made with extra virgin
olive oil rich in polyphenols, their
arteries widened better than after the
same meal made with a refined oil that
had lost most of those compounds. The
longer studies point the same way. In
Córdoba, in southern Spain, researchers
followed 805 people who already had
heart disease.
Half were put on a Mediterranean diet
built around extra virgin olive oil, and
the other half on a low-fat diet. After
1 year, the olive oil group's arteries
widened better. The results were
published in 2020 in the journal PLOS
Medicine, and the improvement showed up
even in people whose arteries had been
in poor shape at the start. So, your
arteries respond to what you eat, meal
by meal, a few hours at a time.
Researchers have also found that a
single heavy meal loaded with saturated
fat can leave the lining less responsive
for several hours afterward. One meal
doesn't decide anything. 20 years of
breakfasts decide a great deal. The last
stop is the one your doctor brings up
every time your blood work comes back.
Cholesterol.
Your body needs cholesterol. It uses it
to build the walls of your cells, to
make hormones, and to make vitamin D.
Cholesterol is waxy, so it can't float
freely in blood. It has to ride in
carriers, and the main carrier is called
LDL.
You can think of LDL particles as
delivery trucks driving cholesterol out
to the places that need it.
The trouble starts when too many trucks
stay on the road for too many years.
Some of them slip through the lining and
get stuck in the artery wall.
The ones that do the most harm are the
trucks that have started to rust.
Doctors call that oxidized LDL.
Rusty particles are the ones the body's
cleanup cells swallow, and those swollen
cleanup cells are what slowly build into
plaque.
Olive oil works on both parts of this
problem. First, the number of trucks.
When the fat from olive oil takes the
place of saturated fat from butter,
cheese, or fatty meat, LDL cholesterol
tends to come down.
Keep those words in mind, takes the
place of. They matter more than anything
else in this lesson.
Second, the rust.
In 2006, a European study called
Eurolive gave 200 healthy men about 2
Tbsp a day of three different olive oils
3 weeks at a time. The oils were alike
in almost every way except one, how many
polyphenols they contained. The more
polyphenols in the oil, the more the
men's good HDL cholesterol went up, and
the more their markers of rusty LDL went
down.
The study was published in the Annals of
Internal Medicine, and European food
regulators later agreed that olive oil
polyphenols help protect the fats in
your blood from this kind of damage as
long as the oil contains enough of them.
Now, about those words, takes the place
of. Ruth is 71, a retired bank teller
from Ohio, and she switched to olive oil
the year her cholesterol first came back
high. She was proud of that switch. She
drizzled olive oil on her toast, on her
baked potato, and on her green beans.
What she never changed was the butter.
The butter went on the toast first and
then the olive oil went on top. Same
with the potato.
Three years later, her cholesterol
hadn't moved and she couldn't understand
why.
When she finally sat down with a
dietitian and wrote out a normal day,
the answer was right there on the paper.
She hadn't swapped anything. She had
added about 3 Tbsp of oil a day, close
to 360 calories on top of everything she
already ate.
Once she let the olive oil replace the
butter instead of joining it, her
numbers started to come down within a
few months.
If you're still with me, tell me in the
comments whether your olive oil has ever
made you cough.
That small detail says a lot about the
bottle in your kitchen and we'll come
back to it. There are plenty of videos
online that promise olive oil will clean
out your arteries, melt away plaque, or
let you stop taking your heart pills.
None of that has been shown in people.
Olive oil has not been proven to
dissolve plaque that's already there. It
won't reopen an artery that's badly
narrowed and it doesn't work like a
blood thinner, even though some of its
compounds affect how platelets behave in
the lab. If you take medicine for your
blood pressure, your cholesterol, or to
prevent clots, talk to your doctor
before changing any medication.
Olive oil belongs alongside those
medicines as one more good habit on the
list. What olive oil does is change the
conditions your arteries live in every
day.
A little less inflammation, fewer rusty
trucks, a lining that opens a little
more easily.
On any single day, you would never feel
it.
Over 10 or 20 years, those small
differences add up and that's what the
biggest studies have measured. The best
known of those studies came from Spain
and it's called PREDIMED.
Researchers there followed 7,447
men and women between 55 and 80.
None of them had heart disease yet, but
all of them were at high risk with
diabetes or several other risk factors.
They were divided by chance into three
groups. One group ate a Mediterranean
diet and received extra virgin olive oil
for free, about a liter a week for the
household.
A second group ate the same kind of diet
with a daily handful of mixed nuts.
The third group was told to cut down on
all kinds of fat. After about 5 years,
the olive oil group had roughly 30%
fewer heart attacks, strokes, and deaths
from heart disease combined than the
low-fat group.
The first report came out in 2013.
Later, problems were found with how
people had been assigned at a few of the
clinics. So, the team reanalyzed
everything and published it again in the
New England Journal of Medicine in 2018.
The main result held up. Then, there's
the American evidence. A Harvard team
looked at more than 93,000 nurses and
other health professionals whose eating
habits had been tracked for as long as
24 years.
People who used more than half a
tablespoon of olive oil a day had about
a 14% lower risk of heart disease and
stroke and an 18% lower risk of coronary
heart disease than people who rarely
used it.
That was published in 2020 in the
Journal of the American College of
Cardiology.
The most useful finding was a smaller
one buried inside that study.
Swapping just 1 tsp a day of butter,
margarine, mayonnaise, or dairy fat for
the same amount of olive oil was linked
to a 5 to 7% lower risk. 1 tsp.
That's a study that watched people
rather than assigning them. So, it can't
prove the olive oil did it. But, it
agrees with what Predimed found in a
controlled trial. And it agrees with the
US Food and Drug Administration. The FDA
allows olive oil to carry a heart claim
on the label, about 2 Tbsp a day, with
one condition written into it.
The oil has to replace a similar amount
of saturated fat without raising the
total calories you eat in a day.
Once again, it comes down to replacing.
So, you have a good oil and a good
reason to use it. Now, let's talk about
what happens to it in an ordinary
kitchen, because this is where a lot of
the benefit gets lost.
Walt is 77, a retired machinist from
Pennsylvania.
For years, he bought olive oil in the
big clear plastic jug from the warehouse
store, because it was cheaper by the
ounce. One jug lasted him most of a
year. And he kept it on the shelf right
above the stove, because that was the
handiest spot.
Last spring, his granddaughter brought
home a small bottle from a farmer's
market and poured some on a plate with
bread. Walt took one bite, coughed, and
told her the oil must have gone bad. She
laughed and told him it was the other
way around. His own oil had no bite at
all. Months of heat from the burners and
light through that clear plastic had
worn most of the good compounds away. It
was still a fine cooking fat, but it
wasn't the oil he thought he was paying
for.
Walt's kitchen holds most of the common
mistakes. The first is the clear bottle.
Light breaks down the polyphenols. Buy
olive oil in dark glass or a metal tin,
and pass on the clear bottles, even when
they're on sale.
The second is the hot spot. The shelf
above the stove or beside the oven is
the worst place for oil. Keep it in a
cool, dark cupboard and put the cap back
on right after you pour because air
wears it down, too.
The third is the giant jug. Olive oil is
at its best when it's fresh. Once a
bottle is open, most experts suggest
using it up within a couple of months. A
smaller bottle that you finish quickly
is worth more than a huge one that sits
for a year.
If the label shows a harvest date,
choose the most recent one you can find.
The fourth is the word light.
On an olive oil label, light describes
the color and the flavor. It has nothing
to do with calories. Light olive oil is
refined with most of the polyphenols
removed and it has the same calories as
any other oil, about 120 in every
tablespoon.
The fifth mistake goes the other way.
Many people were told never to cook with
extra virgin olive oil because it burns.
For ordinary home cooking, that warning
doesn't hold up. A good extra virgin oil
can handle the heat of sautéing eggs,
vegetables, or fish and its natural
antioxidants help protect it while it
cooks. You don't need one oil for
cooking and another for the table. If
the pan starts to smoke, turn the heat
down. Let's put all of this together
into something you can do starting at
your next meal. Step one is choosing the
bottle. Look for the words extra virgin,
dark glass, or a tin and a recent
harvest date. Then, give it the throat
test at home.
Pour a little on a spoon and taste it on
its own.
A peppery catch at the back of your
throat and a slightly bitter edge are
good signs.
Think of that sting as a bonus.
Any olive oil used in place of butter is
still a better trade for your arteries.
Step two is the swap list. Go through a
normal day and find the places where
butter or another solid fat shows up.
Then trade one at a time.
Olive oil in the pan for your morning
eggs instead of butter.
Olive oil and a squeeze of lemon on your
vegetables instead of a pat of butter.
A simple dressing of olive oil and
vinegar instead of a creamy ranch or
blue cheese.
Bread dipped in a small saucer of olive
oil instead of buttered, if bread is
something you enjoy.
>> [snorts]
>> Make one swap this week and another next
week. Step three is the amount. The
studies we talked about point to
somewhere around 1 and 1/2 to 2 Tbsp a
day used in place of other fats.
More doesn't keep adding benefit, but it
does keep adding calories. So for 1 week
measure it. Use a real tablespoon
instead of pouring straight from the
bottle. Most people are surprised by how
fast a free pour adds up. Step four is
good company.
Put your olive oil on the foods it works
best with. Tomatoes, leafy greens,
beans, lentils, fish, and whole grains.
That's the way of eating pretty med
tested and the fat helps you absorb more
of what's in those vegetables. Step five
is the kitchen. Move the bottle away
from the stove today. Keep the cap on.
Buy a size you'll finish in a month or
two. And one more thing. For anyone your
doctor has placed on a special diet, for
example after gallbladder trouble or
with a condition that limits fat, ask
before you add more oil of any kind.
>> [snorts]
>> Olive oil is food and it's still worth
checking how it fits your own plan. So
tomorrow morning, when you pour that
spoonful into the pan, you'll know where
it's going. Let it take the place of the
butter. Keep the bottle away from the
stove and give it the throat test now
and then.
Tell me in the comments which swap
you're going to make first. And if
someone you love is still pouring olive
oil on top of their butter, send them
this lesson. This is Senior Health
Board. Pour it wisely and I'll see you
in the next lesson.

Welcome to Senior Health Board!
Practical, easy-to-understand health and wellness information for adults 60 and older.
On this channel, we focus on healthy aging, mobility, nutrition, sleep, heart health, everyday habits, and common health concerns that can affect quality of life as we get older.
Our goal is simple: turn complicated health topics into clear, useful information you can actually understand and apply in daily life.
No confusing medical jargon. No unnecessary fear. Just straightforward educational content designed to help you make more informed choices about your health and well-being.
Subscribe for regular videos about staying active, independent, and healthier as you age.

This channel is for educational purposes only and is not a substitute for personalized medical advice from your own phy.

records.text:
If You Can’t Walk After Meals, Do This Instead

If you're over 60 and your blood sugar runs high after meals, you've probably been told to take a walk after you eat. Walking after meals does help lower blood sugar spikes, but three walks a day isn't realistic for many older adults. In this lesson, we explain what happens to glucose after a meal, how insulin moves sugar out of your blood and into your muscles, and why post-meal blood sugar spikes become more common with age, even when your fasting blood sugar and A1c look normal.

Your muscles are the biggest place for blood sugar to go after you eat. Insulin opens one door into the muscle, and muscle movement opens a second door that keeps working even with insulin resistance. That's why the right kind of movement after meals can lower blood glucose, reduce how much insulin your body needs, and support better blood sugar control if you have prediabetes or type 2 diabetes.

We count down the five most common after-meal mistakes that keep blood sugar high, from lying down right after dinner to sitting still all evening. You'll also learn about the University of Houston soleus pushup study, a seated calf raise that lowered the blood sugar rise by 52 percent and cut insulin by 60 percent, and the one detail most headlines left out. Then you'll get the After-Meal Reset: a simple routine with a short walk, a safe chair exercise for seniors, and a seated calf move you can do while you watch TV.

Research referenced in this video:
CDC – National Diabetes Statistics Report (diabetes and prediabetes in adults 65+)
CDC – Older Adult Falls data
Hamilton MT, Hamilton DG, Zderic TW. iScience, 2022 (University of Houston, soleus pushup, blood glucose and insulin)
Elek et al. Sports, 2025 (soleus pushup in adults with prediabetes)
DiPietro L et al. Diabetes Care, 2013 (post-meal walking and 24-hour glucose in adults 60+)
Reynolds AN et al. Diabetologia, 2016 (walking after meals in type 2 diabetes)
Buffey AJ et al. Sports Medicine, 2022 (standing and light walking breaks, glucose and insulin)
Gao Y, Finni T et al. Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports, 2024 (squat and walking breaks for glycemic control)
DeFronzo RA, Tripathy D. Diabetes Care, 2009 (skeletal muscle insulin resistance and glucose uptake)

This is education, not medical advice — always check any changes with your own doctor. Talk to your doctor before changing any medication, especially if you take insulin or a sulfonylurea, since extra movement after meals can lower your blood sugar.

Which tool will you try first: walk, chair or heel? Tell us in the comments. If this lesson helped you, subscribe to Senior Health Board and share it with someone you love who's over 60 and watches their blood sugar.

Welcome to Senior Health Board!
Practical, easy-to-understand health and wellness information for adults 60 and older.
On this channel, we focus on healthy aging, mobility, nutrition, sleep, heart health, everyday habits, and common health concerns that can affect quality of life as we get older.
Our goal is simple: turn complicated health topics into clear, useful information you can actually understand and apply in daily life.
No confusing medical jargon. No unnecessary fear. Just straightforward educational content designed to help you make more informed choices about your health and well-being.
Subscribe for regular videos about staying active, independent, and healthier as you age.

This channel is for educational purposes only and is not a substitute for personalized medical advice from your own phy.

records.text:
10 Hygiene Mistakes After 65 That Make You Smell Worse Without Knowing It!

You shower every day, you put on clean clothes, and still a grandchild wrinkles their nose during a hug. If you’re over 65 and you’ve wondered why body odor seems to change with age, this lesson explains what’s really going on. After 40, the skin starts producing a compound called 2-nonenal, which forms when natural skin oil reacts with the air. It doesn’t come from sweat, and water alone doesn’t wash it away. On top of that, our sense of smell weakens with age, so we’re often the last to notice.
In this video we walk through 10 everyday hygiene mistakes that keep the smell around even after a shower. They cover skin oil, sweat, dry mouth and bad breath, tongue coating, polyester clothing, cold laundry washes, a “nose-blind” home, and covering smells with perfume. You’ll also learn three simple at-home checks, the cotton pad test, the spoon test and the door test, plus an easy 15-minute evening routine to help you stay fresh after 60.
This is practical senior hygiene advice for older adults and their families, explained plainly, slowly, one lesson at a time.


Research referenced in this video:
Haze S. et al., Journal of Investigative Dermatology, 2001: 2-nonenal and age-related body odor (Shiseido)
Doty R.L. et al., Science, 1984: Smell identification ability changes with age (1,955 people, University of Pennsylvania)
Callewaert C. et al., Applied and Environmental Microbiology, 2014: Polyester vs. cotton odor (Ghent University)
Furtwangen University, Microorganisms, 2021: Bacteria in low-temperature laundry
Bollen C.M.L. & Beikler T., International Journal of Oral Science, 2012: Tongue coating as the most common cause of bad breath
National Institute of Dental and Craniofacial Research: Dry Mouth and Older Adults
American Academy of Dermatology: Applying antiperspirant at bedtime

Disclaimer: This is education, not medical advice. Always check any changes with your own doctor, and talk to your doctor before changing any medication.

If this lesson helped, subscribe to Senior Health Board for more plain, research-based lessons on health after 60. Tell us in the comments which test you’ll try first, and share this video with someone you love who’s over 60.

Imagine this. It's Sunday afternoon.
There's a pot roast in the oven. And
your daughter Sarah is on her way with
her family. You haven't seen them in
almost a month. And you've been glancing
out the window since lunchtime, waiting
for that familiar car to pull into the
driveway. Finally, the doorbell rings.
Sarah walks through the door with her
arms already open, and you pull her into
one of those long hugs where neither of
you wants to let go first.
Then your 5-year-old grandson, Leo,
comes running down the hallway in his
little sneakers. You scoop him up, hold
him close, and spin him around just the
way he loves. But halfway through that
hug, Leo suddenly leans back. He
wrinkles his nose, looks straight at
you, and says loud enough for everyone
in the room to hear, "Grandpa, you smell
funny." Everyone laughs. He's only five
after all, and children say whatever
pops into their heads without thinking
twice about it. You laugh, too. You
ruffle his hair, pretend it's nothing,
and carry him into the kitchen to show
him the cookies you bought especially
for him. But even as the afternoon goes
on, those four little words keep
replaying in your mind because you
showered just an hour before they
arrived. You put on a freshly washed
shirt. You made sure you were clean and
presentable because your family was
coming to see you. So, how could Leo
notice a smell that you couldn't even
detect yourself. And why does this seem
to happen more often as we get older?
The truth is, it has nothing to do with
how often you shower. After reading a
lot about this, I found that it comes
down to 10 everyday habits. And every
one of them has a simple fix you can
start tonight. And one of them surprised
me more than the rest because part of
the smell Leo noticed isn't coming from
your body at all. It's hiding in your
closet in a place you've never thought
to look. Welcome to Senior Health Board.
Here we take what the research says
about health after 60 and put it up on
the board plainly, slowly, one lesson at
a time. This is education, not medical
advice. So always check any changes with
your own doctor. If lessons like this
are useful to you, please subscribe so
you don't miss the next one. Let's
begin. I'd like to start with a study I
read years ago that has stayed with me
ever since. In 2001, a team of
researchers at the Japanese cosmetics
company Shedo collected skin odor from
people ranging from their 20s to their
70s. And they found a compound called
two nonenol on the skin of people over
40 that simply wasn't there in the
younger group. And the older the person
was, the more of it they tended to find.
Tunanol has a greasy, slightly grassy
smell and it doesn't come from sweat at
all because it forms when the natural
oil on your skin slowly reacts with the
air around it. The easiest way I've
found to picture it is a stick of butter
left out on the kitchen counter, which
looks perfectly fine on the first day,
but after a few days, it starts to smell
a little stale because fat changes once
air gets to it. And the oil on our skin
does something very similar. As we get
older, the mix of fats in that skin oil
shifts and the skin's own protection
against that change gets weaker. So,
more of that stale butter smell forms
and it collects in the oily places which
are the back of the neck, behind the
ears, the chest, and the upper back.
Your own nose gets used to your own
smell within minutes. So, the person
living inside the body is almost always
the last one to notice, which makes this
chemistry and nothing to be ashamed of.
And chemistry is something we can work
with. I'd like you to meet Ruth, who is
71, a retired bank teller from Ohio, who
has showered every single morning of her
adult life, and couldn't understand why
her friends at church had started
sitting one chair farther away at coffee
hour. Mistake number one is letting the
water do the washing on the oily parts
of your body. Most of us were taught to
soap the armpits and the private areas
carefully and then the shower stream
runs over the neck, the shoulders, and
the upper back and we assume that
counts. But water on its own slides
right over oil. The same way rinsing a
buttery frying pan under the tap still
leaves it greasy. That stale butter
compound needs soap, a little lather,
and some gentle rubbing to come off. and
the places it collects are exactly the
places that become hard to reach once a
shoulder gets stiff or the back stops
turning the way it used to. The fix is
simple and it doesn't need any special
product because your usual soap on a
washcloth or a long-handled bath brush
is enough as long as you give the back
of the neck behind both ears, the chest,
and the upper back about 10 slow seconds
each before you rinse. There's a little
test I love for this one because it
takes almost no effort at all. Tonight
before bed, wipe a plain cotton pad
firmly across the back of your neck and
behind one ear. Put it in a small
sandwich bag and smell it in the morning
when your nose is fresh. A lot of people
are surprised by what they find. And
whatever you notice, you've just found
the spot that needs the washcloth. Ruth
tried it and she told her daughter
afterwards that she'd washed her hair
every day for 50 years and had never
once actually soaked behind her ears.
Mistake number two is showering only in
the morning, which feels like the clean
and sensible choice because you start
the day fresh. But think about what
happens over the next 16 hours because
the oil builds up all day long and then
you carry that whole day's worth of oil
into bed and press the back of your neck
into the same pillowcase for seven or
eight hours while the fabric holds the
warmth and the oil keeps reacting with
the air. By morning, the pillowcase is
carrying yesterday and every night you
lie down on it. So are you even after
another shower? You don't have to give
up your morning shower if you love it.
Because what makes the biggest
difference is a short wash before bed.
Even just a warm soapy washcloth over
the neck, the ears, the chest, and the
underarms while you sit on the edge of
the tub, and a pillowcase that gets
changed every 3 or 4 days, which is easy
if you keep a second set in the drawer.
If you've been a morning only shower all
these years and you're going to try the
evening wash tonight, type the word
evening in the comments because I'd
really like to know how many of us have
been doing it the other way round.
Mistake number three is putting your
antipersperent on in the morning. And
this one honestly surprised me when I
first came across it because I think
almost all of us do it right after the
shower and that turns out to be close to
the worst moment of the whole day. An
antipersperent works by forming tiny
plugs at the openings of the sweat
glands and it needs dry skin and a few
calm hours to settle in. But in the
morning after a warm shower, the skin is
still damp and the sweat glands are
already waking up. So a good deal of the
product is carried away by the first
sweat of the day. At night, the body
sweats much less. The skin is dry and
the product has six or eight hours to do
its job, which is why the American
Academy of Dermatology recommends
applying antipersperent before bed. And
many skin doctors say the morning shower
doesn't undo it because by then those
little plugs have already formed.
There's also a difference worth knowing
between the two kinds of sticks on the
store shelf because a deodorant only
covers smell, while an antipersperent
actually reduces the sweat that bacteria
feed on. So, if smell is your worry,
look for the word anti-persperent on the
label. Walter, who is 74 and has lived
on his own since his wife passed 3 years
ago, had bought the same deodorant stick
since the 1980s. and when his daughter
turned it over in the store one day, he
realized it didn't say antipersperent
anywhere on it.
Mistake number four is letting sweat sit
in the places where the air never
reaches. As we get older, many of us
feel the cold more. So, we put on an
undershirt, a sweater, and a cardigan on
top, and we turn the thermostat up a few
degrees. And underneath all of those
layers, the body sweats a little without
ever feeling hot. That sweat ends up in
the places that stay closed all day.
Under the breasts, in the fold of the
belly, in the groin, between the toes,
and on the back of a shirt pressed
against a recliner for an entire
afternoon. Warm, damp skin is exactly
where bacteria like to live. And they
turn plain sweat into that sour smell.
And none of this happens out of neglect
because bending and twisting to dry
those places properly is hard with stiff
hips. so they get a quick dab with the
towel and stay damp. So pat every fold
completely dry after washing, sitting
down to do the feet, and on warm days,
try tucking a thin strip of soft cotton
fabric into a skin fold so that skin
isn't resting against skin, which keeps
that area surprisingly fresh by evening.
It also helps to dress in layers you can
drop the moment the room feels warm, and
to change your socks at lunchtime on
warmer days. If the skin in a fold looks
red, cracked, or shiny, show it to your
doctor because a yeast infection can
settle there and it's usually easy to
treat. If you're still watching, type
the word fresh in the comments. So, I
know these lessons are reaching the
people they're meant for. Mistake number
five is blaming a dry mouth on age. And
I'll admit, I'd always assume the
opposite of what the experts say here.
The National Institute of Dental and
Cranioacial Research is very clear on
this point. Dry mouth is not a normal
part of getting older. And what usually
causes it is medication. Because
hundreds of common medicines reduce
saliva, including many pills for blood
pressure, depression, and an overactive
bladder. Saliva is your mouth's own
rinse cycle, washing bacteria away all
day long. And when there's less of it,
bacteria settle in and the breath turns
stale much faster, especially first
thing in the morning. So, keep a glass
or a bottle of water within reach and
take small sips through the day. Chew
sugar-free gum or suck on a sugar-free
mint after meals to get the saliva
flowing. And if you use a mouthwash,
choose one that says alcohol-free
because alcohol dries the mouth out even
more. A humidifier in the bedroom at
night helps more than most people
expect. If your mouth feels dry most of
the time, bring it up with your doctor
or your dentist. And please talk to your
doctor before changing any medication
because there are often alternatives or
simple treatments that make a real
difference. Mistake number six is
brushing your teeth and forgetting your
tongue. And when I read the numbers on
this one, I actually went back to check
them twice. A clinic in Belgium that
evaluated about 2,000 patients who came
in for bad breath found that the single
most common cause was the coating on the
back of the tongue, which on its own was
behind more than four in every 10 cases.
The surface of the tongue is rough, a
bit like a carpet, so food and bacteria
settle down into it, and a toothbrush
that only cleans the teeth leaves all of
that behind. There's an easy way to
check and you can do it today if you
like because all you need is a teaspoon.
Gently scrape the back of your tongue
with the edge of the spoon. Wait about a
minute and then smell the spoon and
whatever you notice there is close to
what the person across the table notices
when you're talking to them. The fix
takes about 10 seconds because brushing
or scraping the tongue gently from back
to front each night and rinsing
afterwards clears most of that coating
away. If you wear dentures, take them
out at night, brush them, and leave them
to soak because the denture surface
collects the same kind of film, and your
gums deserve a few hours of rest.
Bernie, who is 77 and spent 30 years
delivering mail, tried the spoon test
after noticing that his wife kept
offering him mints after dinner, and he
told her that night he finally
understood what she'd been too kind to
say. If you just tried the spoon test or
you're planning to try it tonight, type
the word spoon in the comments. Mistake
number seven is wearing polyester
against your skin. And this is where I
promise to show you the smell that isn't
coming from your body at all. In 2014,
researchers at Gent University in
Belgium asked 26 people to do an hour of
hard cycling and then collected their
shirts, some made of cotton and some of
polyester. And the next day, a trained
panel smelled them. The polyester shirts
smelled clearly worse. And when the
scientists looked more closely, they
found that one group of odor-
makingaking bacteria called microcatchi
grew much better on polyester than on
cotton. Polyester is a kind of plastic
fiber, and it holds onto skin oil and
those bacteria even after a wash. So, a
shirt can come out of the dryer looking
spotless and still smell like last week
the moment it warms up against your
body. Many of the easy care clothes made
for older adults, the shirts that never
wrinkle, the fleece tops, the slacks,
and the night gowns are polyester or
polyester blends. And a cardigan that
lives in a closet for months can soak up
that stale smell as well. You don't have
to throw anything away because the
simple fix is to check the labels and
choose cotton, linen, or marino wool for
the layer that touches your skin,
meaning your undershirts, your
nightwear, and your underwear, and keep
the polyester for the outer layer where
it touches much less of you. Mistake
number eight is washing everything cold
and quick, which saves energy and works
fine for clothes you've barely worn. The
trouble is that body oil doesn't melt
and lift away in cold water the way it
does in warm water. And a German study
from FKVong University in 2021 found
that low temperature water-saving washes
leave more bacteria behind on laundry.
On top of that, the washing machine
itself can build up a damp, smelly film
in the rubber seal around the door and
in the detergent drawer, and that film
passes a little of itself onto every
load. So, the things that touch your
skin, the undershirts, underwear, socks,
towels, and pillowcases, are worth
washing on the warmest setting their
labels allow with the full amount of
detergent and taking out as soon as the
cycle ends so they don't sit wet in the
drum. Leave the machine door and the
detergent drawer open between washes so
they can dry out. And once a month, run

There's a simple test for this and I

stronger. So cutting back on water makes

tongue along with your teeth. Slip into
something cotton. Lay your head on a
fresh pillowcase and in the morning keep

even if they still look clean. In a

away with good washing, let your doctor

Practical, easy-to-understand health and wellness information for adults 60 and older.

records.text:
5 Medical Checkups I’d NEVER Get After 70 (#1 Is the One Everyone Gets) — Doctor Explains

After 70, some of the most common medical checkups can do more harm than good, especially when you feel perfectly fine. In this video, we look at 5 routine medical tests seniors are often offered at their yearly physical, at a pharmacy or at a church health screening: the whole-body MRI or CT scan, the carotid artery ultrasound, the PSA test for prostate cancer, the urine test without symptoms, and the routine TSH thyroid test that can lead to a thyroid pill for life.
You’ll learn how one small finding on a test can start a chain of follow-up scans, biopsies, antibiotics and new medications, why false alarms become more common after 70, and what the research says about overdiagnosis and overtreatment in older adults. We also cover thyroid medication and bone fracture risk, antibiotics for bacteria in the urine, and PSA screening and biopsy risks after 70.
At the end, you’ll get The Pause Plan, a simple routine to use before your next checkup, along with the questions to ask your doctor about any screening test, so you can decide which tests still make sense at your age.


Research referenced in this video:
Ganguli et al., Cascades of Care After Incidental Findings, JAMA Network Open (2019)
Royce et al., Cancer Screening in Older Adults With Limited Life Expectancy, JAMA Internal Medicine (2014)
Whole-Body MRI Screening in Asymptomatic Adults, Cancer Imaging (2020)
American College of Radiology, Statement on Screening Total Body MRI (2023)
Warren et al., Adverse Events After Outpatient Colonoscopy in the Medicare Population, Annals of Internal Medicine (2009)
US Preventive Services Task Force, Screening for Asymptomatic Carotid Artery Stenosis, JAMA (2021)
US Preventive Services Task Force, Screening for Prostate Cancer, JAMA (2018)
US Preventive Services Task Force, Screening for Colorectal Cancer, JAMA (2021)
Nicolle, Asymptomatic Bacteriuria review (2016)
Infectious Diseases Society of America, Guideline for Asymptomatic Bacteriuria, Clinical Infectious Diseases (2019)
Stott et al., TRUST Trial: Thyroid Hormone Therapy for Older Adults With Subclinical Hypothyroidism, New England Journal of Medicine (2017)
Turner et al., Levothyroxine Dose and Risk of Fractures in Older Adults, BMJ (2011)

Disclaimer: This video is for educational purposes only and is not medical advice. Always talk to your own doctor before changing any test, treatment or medication.

Which of these 5 tests surprised you most? Tell us in the comments, and subscribe for more health lessons for people over 60.

And the way they set it up was very

Carol, 74, a retired church organist

The prescription refilled itself every 3

This is the step that would have caught
